After missing another practice on Friday, Brock Purdy (ankle) is out for Sunday's game against the Seattle Seahawks.

The San Francisco 49ers quarterback is dealing with an ankle injury suffered last week against the Minnesota Vikings. It is not a high ankle sprain, head coach Kyle Shanahan said this week, but Purdy is now set to sit out, leaving Mac Jones with the start. Jones won five of his eight starts last season as Purdy dealt with a toe injury.

Like Purdy, Justin Herbert (concussion) will also be out this week. The Los Angeles Chargers quarterback was placed in protocol after Sunday's loss to the New York Jets and has not progressed enough to play.

"This isn't my first rodeo with regard to starting quarterbacks having an injury you don't know at the beginning of the week when we start game planning," said offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, with DJ Uiagalelei set to start for the 1-9 Chargers after Herbert was ruled out.

Other Week 12 injuries to monitor:

  • Parker Washington has been ruled out for Sunday's game against the Tennessee Titans. The Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver injured his shoulder in practice on Thursday and is considered week-to-week. Running back Bhayshul Tuten (foot/ankle) will also not play. Chris Rodriguez Jr. takes over as RB1.

  • Las Vegas Raiders listed tight end Brock Bowers (ankle) has been listed as questionable after being limited early this week and missing Friday's practice. Bowers missed last week's loss to the Denver Broncos after exiting Week 10 early.

  • Kirk Cousins won't get one of his weapons back in Week 12 as wide receiver Jordan Addison (thumb) remains sidelined. Minnesota Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell said Addison is "progressing well," but he will not be back on the field in Week 12.

  • Tee Higgins (hamstring) woke up sore on Friday morning and did not practice for the Cincinnati Bengals. There is no worry there, head coach Zac Taylor said, as he should be fine for the game against the New Orleans Saints despite the "questionable" designation.

  • Carson Beck (back) is ruled out for the second week in a row while dealing with back spasms. Josh Johnson, who started last week in a blowout loss to the Chiefs, will be starting under center for the Arizona Cardinals yet again.

item.title: Week 12 Preview: Get Right
item.description: Just Win. Excuses? Don’t Care.
item.content:encoded:
The Minnesota Vikings have finished the midseason, four-game gauntlet against preseason playoff and/or Super Bowl favorite teams at 1-3. Not ideal, but not a knockout punch.

Everything but the #1 seed in the NFC is still within reach. The schedule softens considerably. There is no excuse for not leaving the field after the final Week 18 game against the Bears with at least 12 wins.

Next up are the 3-7 Atlanta Falcons at U.S. Bank Stadium. They’re an inconsistent team, but I’d argue they’re better than their record suggests. They have considerable offensive weapons, can be pesky on defense, handed the San Francisco 49ers their only loss of the season, and, of course, gave us a 22-6 loss last year at U.S. Bank Stadium.

Don’t care.

Vikings on Offense

Both Christian Darrisaw and Jordan Addison will miss this game. Don’t care. Shouldn’t matter. The Atlanta Falcons defense is not an elite unit by any stretch: 24th in points, 29th in total yards, 30th in passing yards, 26th in opponent red zone %, 23rd in yards per play, and 20th in rushing yards. I could be missing something, but I don’t see them in the Top 15 in any traditional statistical category.

There’s no reason we can’t get at least 28 points here. The Falcons have allowed 30+ points five times. Their red zone defense has been a major liability, so the Vikings need to convert those trips into touchdowns. I don’t want to see Will Reichard beyond extra points. The king of aura and Fonzie-like charisma should take a backseat this week. He’s missed some kicks recently, so let the guy who largely carried this team for the first six weeks regroup for the stretch run.

Kevin O’Connell needs a dominant 40-point performance to put the critics on ice for another week. Not one like the Bengals game last year, when Isaiah Rodgers and the defense did most of the heavy lifting (similar to Week 1 this year against the Packers, when we came close). I mean, like the performance we last saw against… the Atlanta Falcons… in Week 14 in 2024. Kirk Cousins was the Falcons’ quarterback in that game, so how about he ends up on the winning side and has a game like Sam Darnold’s? Sounds good to me. Heck, that game was 21-21 at the end of the third quarter. I don’t even want it to be close heading into the fourth. Vikings fans need it, but KOC needs it even more. I’m not greedy; I’ll take 31-35 points. Just get it done. No excuses.

Don’t care.

Vikings on Defense

Brian Flores will want to prove that last week’s dud against the 49ers was as rare as a Thanksgiving Day butt-fumble touchdown or as rare as Dan Campbell not going for it on anything less than 4th and 5 in a critical spot.

Our old friend Kevin Stefanski will likely try to replicate Kyle Shanahan’s condensed formations from last week to exploit vulnerabilities in the Flores system. Falcons quarterback Michael Penix can get the ball out quickly, but as ESPN’s Marc Raimondi notes, he has the fourth-worst EPA per dropback under pressure and the worst completion percentage in those situations. Copying what the 49ers did last week could play right into the Vikings’ hands.

It also wouldn’t surprise me if we start to see a bit more man coverage from Flores as we move forward. According to Sharp Football Analysis, the Vikings have played man coverage on only 4.9% of defensive snaps this season, the lowest rate in the NFL. Bumping receivers at the line and disrupting route timing can help address the challenges the 49ers posed last week and prevent the seam plays we’ve been susceptible to this year. Of course, leaning into more man coverage opens you up to other issues, so I’d imagine the key is unpredictability and mixing things up in situations not seen much on tape.

But the key here will be preventing Bijan Robinson from having a game against us like he did last year in the Week 2 loss (143 rushing yards/6.5 YPC, 25 receiving yards). We did a good job holding Christian McCaffrey in check last week (just 62 combined yards from scrimmage), though some of that may have been because Brock Purdy was having a field day on us.

It’s not complicated: stop Bijan Robinson, and you stop the Falcons’ offense. Everything they aim to do depends on Robinson opening up the passing game for Drake London and company. I know we’ll be without Isaiah Rodgers again, but we should still be able to hold the Falcons’ offense in check. No excuses.

Don’t care.

Prediction

This is it, folks. Championship-caliber teams win the next three games: Falcons and Panthers at home, and the Drake Maye-less Patriots. I don’t want to hear any NFL team-on-any-given-Sunday stuff. We need to be 10-3 heading into the Lions rematch, not only for positioning in what’s shaping up to be an incredibly top-heavy, non-NFC East/South playoff picture, but also to keep the collective psyche of Vikings fans from falling headfirst into the pit of despair, with memories of 2003 and 2016 at the forefront of their minds.

We need to make the playoffs at least before we entertain doom and dread this year. The 6-0 start made that mandatory. No excuses.

Don’t care.

Minnesota Vikings: 34

Atlanta Falcons: 14

item.title: Sonny Styles among five Washington Commanders key to beating Cardinals in NFL Week 12
item.description: Count Sonny Styles, Bill Croskey-Merritt among Commanders who must play well vs. Cardinals at State Farm Stadium
item.content:encoded:
The Commanders have won two straight games and are looking for a third on Sunday afternoon against the host Arizona Cardinals. Washington’s in no position to walk into this game overconfident or take Arizona lightly, even with Josh Johnson as starting quarterback. 

Stacking wins is essential for head coach Dan Quinn’s crew, which is entering a relatively soft spot in their schedule.  

They can take sole possession of second place in the NFC East with a win, but they would still be some distance behind the New York Giants.  

Every game’s important now, where the Commanders can’t afford to let opportunities slip. They’ll need players to step against Arizona. Let’s discuss five of them (not named Jayden Daniels) heading into this game.  

LB Sonny Styles 

We could probably put Sonny Styles on this list each week, but it seem appropriate to highlight the No. 7 overall draft pick heading into this game. That’s due to the Trey McBride factor. The Cardinals tight end is a production machine and one of the NFL’s best skill players.  

While Styles won’t be the only player matching up with McBride, but his size (6-foot-5, 243 pounds) and speed and coverage ability makes him uniquely qualified to handle McBride. The Arizona star will still make plays, but Styles could help minimize them a bit. He’ll also be a factor in run defense, as he always is, an important component of the defensive effort when facing a backup quarterback.  

CB Rasul Douglas 

The veteran started a Week 11 win over Cincinnati and played all 58 defensive snaps. He had five tackles and two passes defensed. That type of effort was required with top cornerback Amik Robertson out with an ankle injury.  

That’ll be the case again after weeks working outside primarily in sub packages. The veteran knows what he’s doing and is still good after all these years, calling game with an interception against the Giants in Week 10.  

Another solid performance will be required at Arizona. He’s a ball hawk, and there should be chances for big plays with Johnson at quarterback.  

RB Bill Croskey-Merritt 

While Bill Croskey-Merritt wasn’t Washington’s leading rusher last week, his return from injured reserve should be considered successful. He had 54 yards on 13 rushes (4.2 yards per carry) and a touchdown, plus two catches for 23 yards. Croskey-Merritt’s physical presence provided a lift, especially when Washington worked the ball inside.  

Improvement in the passing game is key to him staying on the field ore.  

“We’ve seen real improvement from him in the pass game, not just in blitz pickup, which is sometimes hard for running backs, but out of the backfield, making plays after he catches the ball,” Quinn said on Friday. “So, that was something that we went into the offseason last year to say, ‘Can that be something more that we’re doing now we’re changing styles of offense?’ I’ve seen that. So, staying healthy, and then the increased awareness in the passing game, because the run game for him, I think is gonna take care of itself.” 

WR Antonio Williams 

The hero of Week 11’s dramatic win over Cincinnati – there was a few of them – is surely looking to build on last week’s momentum. He had nine catches for 122 yards, most of which came on those last two plays to set up Drew Steven’s game-winning field goal as time expired.  

The Commanders need him to stay up and be a true threat alongside Stefon Diggs, especially while Brandon Aiyuk gets ready for game action while on the practice squad.  

DL Tim Settle 

The veteran interior defensive lineman was another standout from the Bengals game, with five tackles and 1.5 sacks. His positive contributions have become essential as Washington survives without Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw.  

He won’t drum up those sacks totals each week, but a stout interior presence against the run and pass, even if it’s absorbing blocks so others can make plays, is a vital component of making this defense perform well as currently constructed.

item.content:encoded:
Week 12 of the NFL season kicked off with a rare Wednesday matchup between the Green Bay Packers and Los Angeles Rams, prepping us for a full Thanksgiving feast that delivered fans a full helping of excitement (and then some). Bears-Lions, Eagles-Cowboys and Chiefs-Bills all came down to the wire, allowing no time for a post-Thanksgiving nap.

The Denver Broncos and Pittsburgh Steelers will face off Friday in a matchup that will have plenty of eyes drawn — even if not for reasons that are entirely due to the actual football being played on the field. Ahead of that matchup, the Steelers made headlines by reportedly benching veteran quarterback and former MVP Aaron Rodgers in favor of backup Mason Rudolph for Week 12 after recent struggles on offense.

This storyline then reached a fever pitch on Wednesday when Rodgers appeared on "The Pat McAfee Show" and went scorched-earth on a rant about head coach Mike McCarthy. Rodgers accused McCarthy of repeatedly falling asleep in meetings and ending a team breakdown with "1-2-3 Let's go Packers." Rodgers was released and officially cleared waivers, now free to sign with any team as a free agent.

We're watching plenty of injuries ahead of the action, including Las Vegas Raiders All-Pro tight end Brock Bowers, who missed Week 11 with an ankle injury, though he was reportedly pushing to play in that matchup. The Jacksonville Jaguars ruled out WR Parker Washington after he suffered a shoulder injury in practice this week, too, which will have fantasy managers looking for other options on the waiver wire.

item.title: Behind Enemy Lines: Seahawks vs. 49ers Week 12 preview
item.description: The Seahawks need a win to stay in the NFC West race, but Brock Purdy's absence won't make the 49ers an easy opponent.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks season is approaching a critical point. A win against the San Francisco 49ers would keep the Seahawks alive in the NFC West race, but a loss would make the division title an extremely difficult proposition and leave the Wild Card as their primary route to the postseason.

Even that path is becoming increasingly complicated. With the NFC North teams putting together strong seasons, Seattle could need 12 wins to have a realistic shot at a Wild Card spot. And the schedule offers little room for recovery, with two games against the Los Angeles Rams, along with the New York Giants, Dallas Cowboys, Philadelphia Eagles and Carolina Panthers still ahead.

There are no Raiders or Cardinals-type games left on Seattle’s schedule. The Rams remain a difficult division opponent, the Giants have shown they can be disruptive defensively, Dallas has an explosive offense despite its defensive struggles, Philadelphia has a talented defense and surprised everyone with the victory on Thanksgiving, and Carolina is having a competitive season with Bryce Young while fighting for the NFC South. Seattle already lost to Washington with its backup quarterback, another reminder that there are no guarantees left on this schedule.

Seattle cannot afford to spend time looking at the standings or calculating playoff scenarios. The Seahawks need to win this game first. Then they can worry about the next one.

Brock Purdy is out, but the challenge remains

With Brock Purdy ruled out, Mac Jones will take over at quarterback for San Francisco. There is some reason for optimism when looking at Mike Macdonald’s history against backup quarterbacks. In 2024, Seattle went 2-0 against teams starting Skylar Thompson and Jimmy Garoppolo, while in 2025 the Seahawks also defeated Jacoby Brissett, who had taken over for an injured Kyler Murray, and Max Brosmer. However, that history is not a guarantee of success. Seattle already lost to Washington with Marcus Mariota starting in place of Jayden Daniels this season, showing that facing a backup doesn’t automatically make the matchup easier.

Jones is also far from an inexperienced backup being thrown into an unfamiliar situation. He went 5-3 as a starter for San Francisco in 2025, throwing for 2,151 yards, 13 touchdowns and six interceptions. He has already demonstrated that he can operate Shanahan’s offense and keep the 49ers competitive without Purdy. The drop in individual talent is real, but Seattle shouldn’t expect the entire offensive operation to suffer because of it.

Perhaps the bigger question is San Francisco’s offensive line, particularly at right tackle. Colton McKivitz suffered a season-ending ankle injury against Minnesota and was replaced by Vederian Lowe, who will now take over as the starter. Lowe was originally brought in as a swing tackle, and Seattle should look to test him with its pass rush, especially if it can create favorable one-on-one situations.

Still, Shanahan’s offensive structure should remain largely unchanged. His system is built around creating favorable matchups, using pre-snap motion and giving quarterbacks defined reads. Expect San Francisco to lean heavily on short passes and quick throws, allowing Jones to get the ball out before Seattle’s pass rush has time to reach him. That approach can limit the impact of the quarterback’s individual limitations while keeping the offense on schedule.

Seattle will need to be disciplined. Attacking Lowe is important, but the defense also has to be ready for an offense designed to neutralize pressure with quick decisions. Purdy’s absence is certainly significant, but between Jones’ previous success as a 49ers starter and Shanahan’s ability to create favorable situations, the Seahawks have plenty of reasons to take this matchup seriously.

Turnovers cannot keep killing Seattle

Seattle was competitive in its previous matchup with San Francisco despite committing multiple turnovers, including two interceptions from Sam Darnold. The Seahawks were still in position to potentially force overtime before the controversial ending, but the mistakes made their comeback much more difficult.

Darnold has thrown nine interceptions in seven games, averaging 1.29 interceptions per game. He is tied for sixth in total interceptions, while his interceptions-per-game rate is the highest among quarterbacks who have played at least seven games. Daniel Jones leads the league in total interceptions with 13, but Darnold’s rate is even more concerning.

The numbers matter even more when looking at Darnold’s rankings across the league. His interception total places him among the league leaders, and his interceptions-per-game rate is even more concerning when accounting for the games he has missed.

Seattle doesn’t need Darnold to win the game on his own. It needs him to protect the football, avoid unnecessary risks and keep the offense from giving San Francisco short fields. Against the 49ers, turnovers could be the difference between a competitive game and a difficult afternoon.

Establishing the run will be easier said than done

Seattle needs to run the football to take pressure off Darnold, but San Francisco presents a difficult matchup up front.

The interior of the 49ers’ defensive line has been effective against the run, making it difficult to consistently gain yards between the tackles. Trying to attack the edges isn’t necessarily an easy alternative, either, with Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw capable of pursuing the ball and closing space quickly.

Seattle has been more effective running between the tackles, including with Zach Charbonnet, so abandoning the middle of the field would be counterproductive. But the Seahawks will need to be smart about how they attack, mixing their concepts and finding ways to create favorable blocking situations instead of repeatedly running into San Francisco’s strength.

The ground game is important for more than just gaining yards. If Seattle can establish it, the offense can control the pace, keep the defense honest and reduce the number of obvious passing situations Darnold has to face.

Seattle must keep San Francisco’s pass rush from taking over

San Francisco’s pass rush hasn’t quite lived up to its reputation in terms of sack production. The 49ers have recorded 17 sacks, placing them near the bottom of the league, but that doesn’t mean Seattle can afford to take the matchup lightly.

Osa Odighizuwa has been an important addition to the defensive front, providing another disruptive presence on the interior. And Nick Bosa is still Nick Bosa. If he hasn’t been producing sacks at the level expected, that only makes him more dangerous heading into a matchup against Darnold.

However, the previous matchup should be a warning for Seattle. The 49ers recorded five sacks against the Seahawks, including four in the first half, and Darnold was brought down five times. Odighizuwa was among those who got to the quarterback, while San Francisco’s defensive front consistently disrupted Seattle’s protection.

Seattle needs to protect the interior, avoid obvious passing situations and prevent Bosa and Odighizuwa from taking over the game. The season sack numbers may not be impressive, but the 49ers have already shown what they can do against this offensive line.

Seattle can’t afford to leave Mike Evans in isolation

Mike Evans dominated Josh Jobe in their previous matchup, winning in just about every way imaginable. He used his strength and physicality, beat him with speed, won through technique, created separation inside and outside, and made plays downfield.

Evans finished with seven catches for 113 yards and a touchdown, including a 28-yard reception that highlighted just how difficult the matchup was for Jobe.

Mike Macdonald has explained the trade-offs involved in providing additional help to Evans, as doubling him can create problems elsewhere in the defense. But Seattle cannot simply repeat the same approach and expect a different result.

The problem is even bigger now with Keenan Allen also in the picture. Allen is another experienced receiver capable of finding openings and exploiting coverage mistakes, and he has already shown a good connection with Brock Purdy despite having limited time with the team.

Seattle needs to find a way to make Evans’ life more difficult without leaving Allen free to take advantage of the attention elsewhere. Jobe cannot be repeatedly left on an island against Evans and expected to win those matchups.

San Francisco can punish Seattle’s aggression

Christian McCaffrey is a major part of the problem, but the bigger question for Seattle is how aggressively it wants to defend the run without compromising the rest of the defense.

Against the Raiders, Seattle was extremely aggressive in trying to stop the ground game, even against an offense that had struggled to run the ball. That approach worked, but San Francisco presents an entirely different challenge. The 49ers have a legitimate running threat in McCaffrey, who can hurt defenses both between the tackles and as a receiver out of the backfield.

McCaffrey doesn’t need much space to turn a routine play into an explosive gain. If Seattle’s linebackers become too aggressive trying to stop the run, San Francisco can take advantage of the space behind them, particularly in the intermediate areas of the field.

This is where Mike Macdonald may need to find a balance. His defense has been excellent, and there is no reason to abandon its core principles. But the Bears and Commanders games showed that Seattle can struggle when an opponent finds ways to exploit its defensive approach. Macdonald may need to be more willing to adjust his aggressiveness and coverage responsibilities depending on the opponent.

With Mac Jones starting, Seattle might be tempted to commit more resources to stopping McCaffrey and forcing the backup quarterback to win through the air. That could be a mistake. Shanahan’s system is particularly effective at creating favorable passing situations, and Jones doesn’t need to play like Purdy to take advantage of openings created by the offense.

Containing McCaffrey while protecting the middle of the field will be one of Seattle’s biggest challenges. The Seahawks cannot allow their commitment to stopping the run to become an opportunity for Jones to attack the spaces behind the linebackers.

Final Thoughts

This is a game that perhaps would have been better positioned for Seattle later in the season, similar to last year’s matchup against the Rams, when the Seahawks had an opportunity to make a statement at a critical point in the playoff race. Instead, Seattle is facing San Francisco now, with very little room left for mistakes.

Purdy’s absence certainly improves Seattle’s chances, but it doesn’t change the fact that the 49ers are a well-coached team with an offense capable of making life difficult for opposing defenses. Mac Jones doesn’t have the same individual talent as Purdy, but Shanahan’s system can still make the offense work efficiently under Jones.

item.title: Falcons with much to prove during the final stretch of 2026
item.description: These Falcons are worth watching closely as the season closes out.
item.content:encoded:
Only seven games remain in the regular season, and we still have more questions than answers about this roster and coaching staff. These are the Falcons that I’ll be keeping a close eye on.

Avieon Terrell

If Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr. get to have their training wheels taken off, why doesn’t Terrell? The Falcons made Avieon their first pick of the Cunningham-Ryan era, but he’s become an afterthought and is losing out during the weekly roster shuffles when he should always be in the deck.

It’s not like the corner hasn’t performed when given the opportunity; he’s been as steady as one could ask of a rookie. Jeff Ulbrich needs to override the special teams-driven decisions and give his rookie the developmental snaps he needs.

Kyle Pitts

One of the most polarizing Falcons in franchise history continues to divide the fan base. You may not be a fan, but you won’t convince me that the player leading the team in receiving touchdowns is useless. Pitts has been a legitimate weapon in the red zone, something fans begged to see for years, but his usage outside of that area has once again called his role on this team into question. Rees doesn’t allow the tight end to stretch his legs until the game is out of hand.

Pitts is eating a heavy diet of screens and short routes, and that doesn’t play into his skill set. If the Falcons can’t get the tight end involved more over these final seven games, then a potential trade should be explored this offseason.

Xavier Watts

Jessie Bates is no longer here, which means Watts has the keys to the backend, but the safety has been in a sophomore slump. He’s still shown flashes of upper-tier safety play, but not enough. Watts’ open-field tackling has been far too inconsistent, and he’s been at the scene of one too many coverage busts. With Bates gone, Watts can play like more of a traditional FS while Hellams slides in as a more traditional SS.

This should help Watts and simplify his responsibilities; he struggled in the box and is better further from the line of scrimmage. The team will need to invest in another safety this offseason, but if Watts finishes the season strong, the team won’t have to spend major capital on his next running mate.

Tommy Rees and Michael Penix Jr.

Fans can’t seem to decide who they dislike more. Penix purists will tell you the OC isn’t giving the quarterback enough opportunities to succeed. At the same time, the other side of the narrative is adamant that the QB is leaving his play caller hanging out to dry with his inaccuracy. Both sides make valid points, but when push comes to shove, one of these two will be dropped if things don’t improve.

Rees has to improve his game flow and stay committed to the run, even if it’s an illusion. Take the 49ers game, for example: the Falcons didn’t dominate on the ground, but they ran Bijan 20 times and threw the ball out of multiple TE personnel groupings at a higher rate than in any other game. The threat of the formation and consistent run plays helped relieve pressure on Penix and the offense, and Rees needs to do more of that. He also needs to adjust his 3rd-down screen rate and force the QB to either make a play or fail trying. He won’t get better on those downs tossing it to poorly blocked screens.

Penix has to hold up his end of the deal and keep the offense on track. His misses have created more timelines than a Marvel movie. Rees has schemed up opportunities for the quarterback, but he isn’t cashing in on them, and it’s exasperating the offense’s lack of flow. When Penix is off schedule, everyone is, and his confidence is in shambles right now.

He has to be better at managing pressure; when accounting for throwaways, he’s still off target more than anyone, and that’s a critique fans are tired of hearing. He isn’t going to be a volume shooter in this offense, and that means he needs to be efficient from start to finish. He’ll never be under a bigger microscope than he will in these last 7 games.

James Pearce Jr.

Probably not good that his suspension ended 2 weeks ago and hardly anyone has noticed. The troubled defender got a slap on the wrist for his offseason antics, and now he needs to prove to the team he can be a professional and grow as a person. However, a mysterious back injury seems to be holding him back, and that’s a problem for a player who needs to keep developing. 10.5 sacks is nothing to stick your nose up at, but half of those were cleanup sacks, and Pearce was the worst run-defending edge on the team.

Many of us remember that magical Vic Beasley season and know how numbers can be deceiving. Pearce can’t live off his rookie season forever, but if this back keeps limiting him to 15 snaps a game, the team might shut him down early.

Some players listed aren’t as worried about their futures as others, but that doesn’t make their development any less important over this final stretch. Atlanta needs to get the best look at each because all of them can influence how Atlanta attacks the offseason. Who will you be watching the most?

item.title: Cowboys vs. Eagles: The good, the bad, and ugly from Week 12
item.description: Any Cowboys good from Thanksgiving is basically forgotten due to all of the bad.
item.content:encoded:
To say the Dallas Cowboys completely embarrassed themselves with the 39-38 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles on Thanksgiving is an understatement. This was a game they were in complete control of until they had a meltdown in the fourth quarter allowing the Eagles to come back and win with a last-second field goal.

Hopefully the Cowboys embarrassing loss didn’t leave a sour taste in your mouth ruining your Thanksgiving meal because this Week 12 loss has to be one of the biggest letdowns many of us have witnessed from this organization. There was a lot of good for Dallas in this matchup, but sadly all of the bad and ugly made it all but meaningless.

THE GOOD – CeeDee Lamb/Quinnen Williams

Week in and week out CeeDee Lamb and Quinnen Williams are continually proving why they are considered among the best that their positions. Both are playing at a consistent All-Pro level this season and are quite possibly having the best year of their careers despite playing on a bad team. 134 receiving yards on seven catches has No. 88 at 1,242 yards on the season, putting him well on pace to shatter his season best in 2023 (1,749). And, with another QB sack Sunday, No. 92 nine so far this year means he could break his 12-sack season in 2022.

THE BAD – Cowboys’ fourth-quarter meltdown

Entering the fourth quarter Sunday afternoon the Cowboys had a comfortable lead leading the Eagles 31-17. For most teams around the league that usually equates to victory, but sadly not for the Cowboys. Dallas was able to put seven more points on the board, but allowed the Eagles to score 22, including a last-second field goal that secured the 39-38 victory. We can point the finger at players and coaches alike that led to this meltdown, but we can probably be all agree the majority of the blame lands at Brian Schottenheimer’s feet.

THE UGLY – QB Joe Milton’s torching of the Dallas defense

The Cowboys defense was able to sack Joe Milton five times Sunday afternoon, but he ended up getting the better of them in the end, picking apart the secondary and making them look absolutely ugly. The Cowboys castoff, and the Eagles third QB of the year, ended up throwing for 331 yards and four touchdowns in this Week 12 matchup. He’s the latest backup QB to shred Dallas’ secondary this season and may or may not be the last. Regardless of what his future may be in the league, he completely embarrassed his former teammates on Thanksgiving.

item.title: Cleveland Browns: Remembering their two Sunday night wins
item.description: Cleveland brings a 2-11 regular-season record on Sunday night into this week’s game. Remembering those two wins.
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns make their return to Sunday Night Football this week as they host the Las Vegas Raiders.

It has been five years since the NFL deemed the Browns worthy of a Sunday night game, with the last appearance resulting in a 16-10 loss to the Baltimore Ravens in Week 12 of the 2021 season in a game where the Browns intercepted Baltimore quarterback Lamar Jackson four times.

The last time it was a home game? That was in 2019, when the Browns lost 20-13 to the Los Angeles Rams, as Cleveland’s late comeback fell short after the Browns were unable to convert a first-and-goal with less than a minute remaining.

This will be just the 14th time the Browns will be playing on a Sunday night in the regular season, with the first game coming in 1984 when they faced the Denver Broncos in a special edition of Monday Night Football. 

Cleveland is just 2-11 in their previous appearances, so let’s take a look back at those two victories.

Browns 33, Steelers 13 (October 5, 2003)

Cleveland’s maiden win on a Sunday night was also the last time they won a regular-season game in Pittsburgh. 

Quarterback Tim Couch threw touchdown passes to André Davis and Kevin Johnson to give the Browns a 16-3 lead early in the second quarter. The Steelers pulled within six points after a one-yard touchdown run by Jerome Bettis, but Couch smartly moved the Browns down the field and scored on a nine-yard touchdown run to send the Browns into halftime with a 23-10 lead.

Cleveland’s defense essentially shut down any hopes that Pittsburgh had for a comeback when cornerback Daylon McCutcheon picked off quarterback Tommy Maddox and returned it 75 yards for a touchdown just five minutes into the second half.

Couch finished the game by completing 20-of-25 passes for 208 yards and two touchdowns in what turned out to be the last highlight of his career.

Browns 20, New York Giants 6 (December 20, 2020)

Cleveland moved to 10-4 on the season after taking down the Giants in a game flexed into the Sunday night time slot.

Quarterback Baker Mayfield led the Browns on a pair of 95-yard touchdown drives as he finished 27-of-32 for 297 yards and touchdown passes to Jarvis Landry and Austin Hooper. Running back Nick Chubb capped off the scoring for Cleveland with a one-yard touchdown run in the fourth quarter.

Cleveland’s defense limited quarterback Colt McCoy, starting in place of the injured Daniel Jones, to just 221 passing yards, and the Giants finished with just 288 yards of total offense.

The win moved Cleveland closer to their first playoff berth since 2002 and was their first season with double-digit wins since 2007.

Sunday nights have not been kind to the Browns over the years, but this week’s game against the Raiders presents a huge opportunity for Cleveland. Win, and the Browns not only stay firmly in the playoff race in the AFC, but also set up a showdown next week with the Cincinnati Bengals for first place in the AFC North.

The Browns have been waiting five years to be back on Sunday night. Time to show the nation what they have been missing.

item.title: 2027 NFL Draft prospects for the Giants in Rivalry Weekend – Saturday
item.description: Which 2027 NFL Draft prospects should NY Giants fans be watching on Saturday’s rivalry games?
item.content:encoded:
Good morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome back to Rivalry Week 2026!

We already talked about some of the best players from Friday’s slate of games, so now we’re on to Saturday. We have some of the biggest games and the best rivalries in sports today. And one of the best parts of the “Transfer Portal Era” is that we’re getting more “good against good” matchups than ever before.

As always, we’re going to use college football and the NFL Draft as a lens through which to look at the Giants. So we’ll be sticking to prospects that fill the Giants’ needs as they’re currently perceived.

Syracuse vs. (4) Notre Dame

ABC – noon

Syracuse player to watch – Chris Peal (CB)

We don’t talk about ‘Cuse all that often, but Peal is an intriguing player. He was a four-star recruit who spent the first two years of his career at Georgia before transferring to Syracuse. Peal has NFL traits at 6-foot-1, 200 pounds with good speed and play strength. He has solid fluidity, as well as good instincts in zone coverage and run defense. Peal has the traits to be a good press-man corner as well, but he hasn’t played up to his potential yet. He could be a great developmental prospect for the Giants if he slips to them on Day 3.

(4) Notre Dame player to watch – Jordan Faison (WR)

The Giants should be watching the entire Irish secondary. They (probably) won’t have a chance at CB Leonard Moore, and their secondary is in a great place right now. However, it’s a unit with high attrition and subpackages require a lot of DBs.

That said, I want to take a look at a player who could be matched against Peal.

Faison has exploded onto the national scene as a senior and has 56 receptions for 724 yards and 7 touchdowns. He doesn’t have great size at 5-foot-11, 185 pounds, with great speed, quickness, and ball skills. Faison primarily plays out wide but could play inside as well. He tracks the ball extremely well, has the ups to high-point the ball, and also has upside as a punt returner.

(7) Miami vs. Boston College

ESPN – noon

(7) Miami player to watch – Ahmad Moten Sr. (iDL)

We’ve talked about both of the Miami defensive tackles before, and they’re both worth watching this game. Moten Sr. is slightly smaller (listed at 6-foot-3, 300 pounds), however he plays with consistent pad level and power as well as the quickness to win as a pass rusher. He can play on the nose despite his weight, as well as play at a 3 or 4i technique. Moten will likely land as a Day 2 prospect, though he could be a fringe first rounder for the right team after a strong draft process.

Boston College player to watch – Kris Jones (OLB)

Jones originally enrolled at Georgia in 2024, but didn’t appear all that often before transferring to BC for the 2026 season. Jones has eligibility remaining, so it might behoove him to return to school and continue to develop. As things stand now, he will likely find his way onto the field as a special teams player while he continues to develop as a linebacker. Teams will likely view the 6-foot-2, 240-pound Jones as more of a WILL with pass rush upside than as a full-time edge defender.

Kentucky vs. (19) Louisville

ESPN2 – noon

(19) Louisville player to watch – Isaac Brown (RB)

The Giants definitely need a more explosive element out of their backfield, and Brown could certainly supply that. He’s a small back at 5-foot-9, 190 pounds, but boasts elite quickness, agility, and explosiveness. Brown has the ability to cut on a dime, stick his foot in the ground, and be at top speed almost instantly. He also has great vision to identify holes as well as anticipate defenders. He’s averaged 7.5 yards per carry over his three years at Louisville, including an incredible 8.8 yards per carry last year.

Kentucky player to watch – C.J. Baxter (RB)

Another running back to watch in this game, Baxter is much more of power back than Brown at 6-foot-1, 230 pounds. He started at Texas before transferring to Kentucky after injuries derailed the start of his college career. Baxter has the potential to be an every-down back, with untapped upside as a pass catcher as well as his ability as a rusher. He might not have blazing speed, but he does hit top speed quickly, which can make him tough to bring down thanks to his size and contact balance.

Baxter’s size and versatility could make him appealing to a Giants team looking for a “bell cow” back.

Clemson vs. South Carolina

ESPN2 – 3 p.m

Clemson player to watch – Elliott Washington II (CB)

Washington is the other corner at Clemson across from Ashton Hampton, who could well be a Top 10 pick. Washington is an interesting player with rare speed and ball skills with 5 interceptions and 7 passes defensed this year. He started his career at Penn State before transferring to Clemson after James Franklin was fired. Like most former Penn State players, Washington could still use development in the finer points of playing his position, but he has rare ball skills and a team will want to find ways to get him on the field.

South Carolina player to watch – Dylan Stewart (EDGE)

Stewart’s draft stock has been an absolute rollercoaster this year. He started out as a Top 5 player, before his draft stock began to drop due to questions about his lack of production. It then fell off a cliff when he was suspended by both South Carolina and the NCAA for his actions after completely losing his temper. Stewart’s draft stock could be incredibly volatile, so he could go in the Top 10, or he could fall to the bottom of the first round.

After returning, Stewart has played much more under his control and has played some of the best football of his career. He’s long, fluid, fast, and explosive, with the ability to simply take over games when he’s on his game. The Giants’ incredible depth at edge defender has been one of the real strengths of their team this year, and they could look to reinforce it if Kayvon Thibodeaux leaves via free agency.

(1) Georgia vs. Georgia Tech

ABC – 3:30 p.m.

(1) Georgia player to watch – Jordan Hall (iDL)

Hall is going to be an intriguing prospect in a deep defensive tackle class. He’s a big, powerful nose tackle could appeal to the Giants at 6-foot-4, 320 pounds and has significant upside as a run defender who could also contribute to the pass rush. The intrigue comes from the fact that despite being a senior who has been playing real snaps since his freshman year, he only played 14 total games in 2024 and 2025 due to injury. He dealt with stress fractures in 2024 and a knee injury in 2025, but is back to full strength in 2026 and has emerged as a stalwart in the middle of a great Georgia defense this year.

Georgia Tech player to watch – Justice Haynes (RB)

Haynes is a well-travelled senior who started his career at Alabama in 2023, then transferred to Michigan for the 2025 season, and is now at Georgia Tech. He has solid size at 5-foot-10, 210 pounds and has been a productive runner at each of his stops. He has a career 6.1 yards per carry average, averaging 5.9 yards per carry at Alabama, 7.1 YPC at Michigan, and 5.4 YPC at Georgia Tech. It’s notable that he’s produced at three different schools, each with different offensive lines, blocking schemes, and offensive schemes. Haynes is a fluid runner who has the feet to pick his way through the trash and is very difficult for defenses to bring down cleanly. He’s averaging 4.2 yards after contact this year after averaging 3.5 yards after contact last year.

(8) Wake Forest vs. Duke

ESPN – 3:30 p.m.

(8) Wake Forest player to watch – Carlos Hernandez (WR)

We highlighted Hernandez here last week, and we’re going to do so again this week. Wake Forest has stormed onto the national scene and Hernandez is one of the primary focuses of their offense. He has only average size at 6-foot, 190 pounds, but he has been consistently productive for the Demon Deacons and is currently 6th in the country in receiving yardage. Every year there’s a with unassuming traits who has the potential to take the NFL by storm if he gets the right opportunity. This year that might be Hernandez.

Duke player to watch – Jeremiah Hasley (TE)

Tight end isn’t a dire need for the Giants, but considering how often they use multiple TE sets, they could look to to another late round prospect to add competition. Hasley has solid size at 6-foot-5, 250 pounds, and is a capable receiver as well as blocker. He’s a high-effort player who’s a reliable safety blanket for his quarterback as well as a solid blocking tight end. Hasley is a former linebacker and has only been playing tight end full time since 2023, so he still has plenty of upside with development.

(9) UCLA vs. (15) USC

CBS – 3:30 p.m.

(9) UCLA player to watch – Scooter Jackson (S)

I’ve already talked about Bruins’ running back Wayne Knight and believe that he’s a player everyone should be watching, so I want to take this opportunity to shine a light on the UCLA defense.

UCLA comes into this game as one of the biggest surprises in college football, boasting a 10-1 record despite losing their starting QB (Nico Iamaleava) in his fifth start. Their defense has been a big reason for their success, and their ability to take the ball away in particular. Safety Scooter Jackson leads the Bruins’ defense — and the Big10 — with 5 interceptions as well as a forced fumble, and has also returned one of those picks for a touchdown. He’s also 6th in the Big10 with 9 passes defensed on the season as well. Jevon Holland is one of the best safeties in the NFL this year, and they’ve gotten very good play from Ar’Darius Washington and Jason Pinnock as well. That said, the Giants could be interested in having more young talent in the pipeline to keep the level of play high.

(15) USC player to watch – Jide Abasiri (iDL)

USC left tackle Elijah Paige and QB Jaden Maiava will get most of the attention in this game. However, the Giants are pretty well set at quarterback, and it’s probably too early to draft a developmental tackle highly with both Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor in place for the foreseeable future.

So we’re turning to the defensive side of the ball and Jide Abasiri. We have, for the most part, looked at defensive linemen with nose tackle upside for the Giants. However, it’s certainly possible that they’re set there for a good long while with both Bobby Jamison-Travis and C.J. Okoye in the fold. Abasiri profiles as much more of a defensive end or under tackle who can play the 5-technique, 4i, or 3-technique depending on the down, distance, and package called. He’s a powerful player at 6-foot-5, 280 pounds with the room on his frame to add weight if necessary. Abasiri is a better run defender than pass rusher right now, and could be a player in the mold of Chauncey Golston.

(10) BYU vs. Cincinnati

Fox – 3:30 p.m.

(10) BYU player to watch – LJ Martin (RB)

There are a lot of different ways we could go with this BYU squad, but LJ Martin makes sense in the context of how focused the Giants have been on the running back position since free agency.

Martin has been limited by ankle injuries this year, but is a force when he’s healthy. He’s a physical downhill runner at 6-foot-2 and 225, and is a very difficult player to bring down. He has very good vision and patience behind the line of scrimmage, as well as excellent contact balance and surprising agility for such a big player. Martin is averaging 4.5 yards per carry after contact and 6.6 yards per carry overall. He’s also a useful player in the passing game, with great upside as a pass protector while also being an underrated receiver out of the backfield. Martin lacks home run speed, but everything else about him says “every-down Bellcow”.

Cincinnati player to watch – Evan Tengesdahl (LG)

We’ve mentioned Tengesdahl before, and it bears repeating. The Cincinnati offensive line is probably the most interesting unit on their team from a Giants’ perspective, and the left guard spot is the most in need of an upgrade for the Giants.

The contract extension signed by Jon Runyan Jr. this year could make it difficult for the Giants to move on from him, but it’s still something they could consider after the season. Tengesdahl is a squat, powerful guard at 6-foot-3, 325 pounds with obvious power in his upper and lower body. He has the potential to be a mauler in the run game as well as a reliable pass protector against most defensive tackles. The Giants should probably consider leaving Sisi Mauigoa at right guard to fully develop and finding a right tackle of the future later on, so pairing Mauigoa with a player like Tengesdahl could give them a very formidable interior.

Vanderbilt vs. (5) Tennessee

ESPN – 7 p.m.

Vanderbilt player to watch – Junior Sherrill (WR)

Sherrill is probably the Commodores’ best prospect this year, and the one most scouts will be watching this year. He’s a compact, twitchy receiver at 5-foot-11, 200 pounds, and is a threat at every level of the defense. He has the agility to uncover quickly for short passes as well as the ball skills to produce on intermediate and deep routes. He will likely excel in offenses that put receivers in position to create yards after the catch, and could be a real weapon in a “Shanahan-McVay” scheme. With that in mind, it’s a question as to whether a team like the Giants are the best fit. However, he’s also improved every year in college and can probably be a productive player for any offense.

(5) Tennessee player to watch – Arion Carter (LB)

I’ve been wanting to talk about Carter for a while, and this is a great opportunity. The Giants’ linebacking corps is the deepest and most talented its been in decades, but they should still consider Carter if he’s available. Not only is he a great player, he is a (by all accounts) a great human. Carter’s girlfriend, an ICU nurse, was diagnosed with cancer early this year and he has publicly supported her through her fight. He now makes a donation to cancer research for every play he makes, from $427 for a tackle and $500 for a sack, to $1,000 for a turnover and $5,000 for a defensive touchdown — So far he’s donated over $30,000.

The $427 amount is a reference to the two games he was suspended at the start of the season by the NCAA for accepting a $427 flight from an agent last year when he briefly declared for the draft before returning to school (and paying the agent back).

On the field, Carter is a menace. He’s a bit undersized at 6-foot-1, 235 pounds, but he has a sky-high football IQ, a wide-open motor, and the athleticism to cover a lot of ground at the second level. He’s been highly productive this year (as you could guess from his donation total), notching 76 total tackles, 11.0 tackles for a loss, 5.0 sacks, 1 forced fumble, 1 pass defensed, and 3 fumble recoveries. His draft stock will be interesting to follow over the winter and spring, but his character and ability on the field could make him very attractive to the Giants wherever he lands on their board.

(6) Alabama vs. Auburn

ABC – 7:30 p.m.

(6) Alabama player to watch – Ryan Coleman-Williams

It’s honestly difficult to highlight a single Alabama player, and rather than try to separate a single defender from a thoroughly talented defense, I’m going to the offensive highlight.

Ryan Coleman-Williams exploded onto the national scene as a true freshman, taking the country by storm. He was unable to maintain the torrid pace of his freshman campaign and took a step back as a sophomore, struggling mightily with consistency. He’s rediscovered his consistency this year, and with it his confidence, and has returned to his 2024 form.

Coleman-Williams has a similar build and skillset as Malik Nabers at 6-foot, and roughly 185 pounds (though he could certainly come in heavier at the Combine), with simply electric quickness and speed. He has the type of twitch to allow him to separate at will on underneath routes or pick up chunk yardage on run-after-catch opportunities, and the speed to blow the top off a defense on vertical routes. He’s a surprisingly physical and competitive receiver, with unexpected ability as a blocker in the run game or on screen passes.

Concerns about Coleman-Williams’ consistency and ball skills could drop him in an absurdly deep receiver draft, but that could also make him an absolute steal for a team that believes in him and is able to develop him.

Auburn player to watch – Keshaun Singleton (WR)

I was tempted to go with iDL Cody Sigler here, and he’s definitely worth keeping an eye on as a later-round defensive tackle prospect. That said, Alabama boasts one of the best defenses — and defensive secondaries in particular — in college football. That makes this an excellent opportunity for WR Keshaun Singleton to boost his draft stock.

Singleton is similar to Malachi Fields as a big-bodied outside receiver at 6-foot 220 pounds, with good suddenness out of his breaks for a big receiver and strong hands at the catch point. He also doesn’t have great deep speed, but is able to create separation with his route running. Singleton has a career-high 58 catches after transferring from South Florida to Auburn this year, and has currently tied his career-high 8 touchdowns. He could be a name to watch on the third day of the draft.

(12) Oregon vs. (24) Washington

NBC – 7:30 p.m.

(12) Oregon player to watch – Iapani Laloulu (OC)

The Giants like Bryan Hudson at center, but they could also decide to find competition for the spot or an outright upgrade. If so, Iapani Laloulu (nicknamed “Pancho”) is a player to keep an eye on. He’s played both left and right guard as well as center for the Ducks, but he’s excelled at center since moving there last year. He has great natural leverage and a powerful frame at 6-foot-2, 325 pounds, and at least as much play strength as his frame would indicate. While many centers tend to be lighter and use positioning and technique to beat bigger nose tackles, Laloulu meets them on their own turf and plays with a mauling mentality. He’s capable of distorting the line of scrimmage and is very difficult to uproot and move off the ball when he’s playing with good leverage.

Greg Roman wants to be able to run downhill and between the tackles, and that could make Laloulu very attractive to the Giants.

(24) Washington player to watch – Alex McLaughlin (S)

Washington is another school that’s a bit frustrating from a scouting perspective. They have intriguing players, but few of them are draft eligible this year, and their most intriguing player — Demond Williams Jr. — is a quarterback.

McLaughlin, however, is both a senior and an interesting safety prospect. He has great size for the position at 6-foot-2, 205 pounds and currently leads the Huskies in tackles (79), tackles for a loss (9.5), sacks (3.0), forced fumbles (1), passes defensed (8), and interceptions (3). He’s a physical downhill player (as you can tell from his tackle production) as well as natural ballhawk who has produced against the pass in each of the last two years and also as a pick-six in both 2025 and 2026. Considering how well McClaughlin adapted when he transferred to Washington from FCS level Northern Arizona, it’s likely that he’ll either see his draft stock rise considerably over the coming months or that he’ll far out-play his draft slot.

item.title: Survey results: Fans confident Seahawks will best 49ers
item.description: Despite currently sitting outside the playoffs, Seahawks fans aren’t giving up on the defending champs.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks can move themselves into the NFC playoff picture by beating their divisional rival, the San Francisco 49ers, on Sunday. If you ask a Seahawks fan, they’ll probably say that Seattle will win that game, at least according to our Seahawks Reacts survey results.

When asked if the Seahawks would beat the 49ers in the pivotal matchup, 50% of fans said the 6-4 team would upset the current No. 1 seed in the NFC. It should be noted that this survey was taken before the 49ers ruled out starting quarterback Brock Purdy, so in all likelihood this percentage of fans has only grown since Friday afternoon’s announcement.

Here are the full results:

Seahawks fans’ confidence in an upset isn’t entirely unfounded, as Seattle has fared much better against the Bay Area team since they hired Mike Macdonald, especially in Santa Clara. Macdonald’s defense has proved that it can stop a Kyle Shanahan-led offense before, including in Week 18 of the 2025 season, where the Seahawks held the 49ers to just 3 points.

The Seahawks have won their last three games at Levi’s Stadium, including Super Bowl 60, giving them some confidence heading on the road. Seattle is also coming off a bye week, while San Francisco is coming back from a trip to Mexico City against a physical Minnesota Vikings team, which might contribute to the confidence of fans.

Notably, Seahawks fans aren’t entirely behind their team, with 36% predicting a 49ers’ victory and 17% projecting it to be by two scores. The 49ers haven’t beaten the Seahawks by two scores since Macdonald’s first season as head coach on Oct. 10, 2024, when they won 36-24 at Lumen Field.

One thing is clear from the survey results, though: fans expect this game to be close and once again decided by one score as their first meeting was.

In addition to the 49ers question, fans were once again polled on whether they thought the franchise was moving in the right direction.

This result is a solid mark for a 6-4 team on the playoff bubble heading into December, but is also a puzzling one with context. Last week, 74% of Seahawks fans were confident the team was trending positively, and the team didn’t play a game on Sunday, meaning something over the bye week has fans a little more shook than they were a week ago.

Perhaps that has something to do with the 49ers’ thrashing of the Vikings on Sunday night, which positioned them as midseason Super Bowl favorites. It could also be the continued emergence of the NFC North, which has had a hold of three of the seven playoff spots for most of the year.

With the Seahawks sitting idle, maybe the realization that the defending champs will need a near-perfect second half to make the playoffs became a little more real.

I’d lean toward the last of the three reasons, but there’s certainly plenty of theories to concoct as to why confidence has dropped in the organization without the team playing a game. Either way, Sunday’s game will surely change that number in a massive way as the Seahawks take their playoff hopes to Santa Clara to face Mac Jones’ 49ers.

Let us know what you think of the results and drop your theories of why fans don’t trust the organization as much after the bye week in the comments below!

item.title: Steelers WR DK Metcalf fined by NFL
item.description: Steelers WR DK Metcalf fined for his ejection vs. Eagles.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers rallied the troops and dominated the AFC West-leading Denver Broncos on Black Friday in Acrisure Stadium, 27-5. However, less than 24 hours after the win, the Steelers’ top receiver is back in the headlines after being fined by the NFL for his actions during the team’s Week 11 contest against the Philadelphia Eagles.

Tom Pelissero of The Ringer reported on Saturday that the league has fined Metcalf a total of $26,867 for several infractions that occurred during the Steelers’ Week 11 game. The receiver was ejected from the Steelers game against the Eagles after receiving his second personal foul of the game for an altercation with Philadelphia defensive back Cooper DeJean.

It looked as though Metcalf was trying to poke the eyes of the defensive back, but the receiver has denied those allegations. Although Metcalf has not been clear about what exactly transpired on the field, it landed him in the headlines for all the wrong reasons.

The game marked the third ejection in the career of Metcalf, his first since 2023 and his first as a Steeler. Some expected Metcalf to receive a suspension from the league office for the repeat offense, but the league said he would not be suspended and could still face fines. The large fine we see today will be the only punishment Metcalf faces for his Week 11 actions.

The receiver made his mark yesterday with a spectacular touchdown catch on Broncos standout cornerback Patrick Surtain in the Steelers’ dominant win and used sign language to say, “keep standing on business 4.”

item.title: Can Puka Nacua return to Rams this year?
item.description: Puka Nacua news and other news aroundf the Rams and NFL on a Saturday
item.content:encoded:
The Puka Nacua injury is fascinating in terms of the varying reports to how long it will take him to recover. At this point, sit back and see what happens. It seems no one knows how long Puka will be out, when he’ll be back, how long he’ll be a Ram via extension or not. It’s fascinating.

Report: Rams haven’t completely ruled out Puka Nacua returning in playoffs (ramswire)

“On Saturday, though, Tom Pelissero of The Ringer shared a new update that the Rams “haven’t completely closed the door on Puka Nacua returning in the playoffs.” That being said, the Rams “aren’t expecting” to get him back for the postseason, which is essentially what McVay said in the first place.“

NFL insider shares unexpected optimistic Puka Nacua update for Rams (sportingnews)

“The Rams haven’t completely closed the door on Puka Nacua returning in the playoffs,” Pelissero reports. “But they aren’t expecting to get their star receiver back from surgery for a complete MCL tear that wasn’t a routine injury.”

This is an interesting update for the Rams with Nacua. While the team is expecting Nacua to miss the rest of the regular season and all of the playoffs, a late playoff return isn’t totally impossible.

His surgery will take months to recover from, but if the Rams could make a run to the Super Bowl, Nacua might have a small chance of suiting up by then if his recovery is going well and he’s ahead of schedule.“

Dianna Russini reveals NFL GMs’ thoughts on Puka Nacua’s long-term future with LA Rams (sports.yahoo)

“Puka Nacua has been a revelation since the LA Rams drafted him in 2023, setting rookie records with 105 catches for 1,486 yards. He has since become a two-time Pro Bowler and first-team All-Pro, with 383 catches, 4,906 yards and 23 receiving TDs through 2026, including a league-leading 129 receptions and 1,715 yards in 2025.

This season, before his season-ending injury, Nacua posted 70 receptions for 715 receiving yards and 4 receiving touchdowns across 7 games played. His on-field production has never been an issue, yet his future remains uncertain. Playing out the final year of his rookie contract, Nacua is a free agent this coming offseason, and there is some speculation about his future within the league’s power circles.“

Rams not giving up hope for Puka Nacua returning from injury in time for playoffs (clutchpoints)

“Puka Nacua’s 2026 NFL season has been a tale of production derailed by injury and off-field discipline. Before his injury, the fourth-year wideout remained Matthew Stafford’s most reliable chain-mover and high-volume target. He appeared in seven games and racked up 70 receptions for 715 yards and four touchdowns. However, Nacua’s year was persistently interrupted by lower-body ailments. These culminated in Week 9 when he suffered a complete MCL tear in his right knee. Nacua eventually underwent MCL surgery during the Rams’ Week 11 bye. That procedure carries a four-to-five-month recovery timeline. It also leaves Los Angeles bracing for the remainder of the 2026 regular season and likely the playoffs without its premier playmaker.“

Rams get bad news about two injured tight ends (ramswire)

“ESPN’s Adam Schefter reported that Tyler Higbee suffered a chest contusion that will leave him week to week. Meanwhile, ESPN’s Ian Rapoport reported that Davis Allen suffered a high-ankle sprain during Wednesday night’s win. Both tight ends left the game against Green Bay and did not return.

Higbee reportedly has a chance to play in Week 13 against the Kansas City Chiefs, while Allen’s injury needs more evaluation before truly understanding how long he could be out.“

Report: Davante Adams return still ‘at least a couple of weeks away’ (sports.yahoo)

“Now, Tom Pelissero of The Ringer has reported Adams is still “at least a couple of weeks away” from returning.

And while the Rams still are confident that receiver Davante Adams will play again this season after undergoing surgery last month on a ruptured hamstring, Adams’s return is still at least a couple of weeks away.

That suggests Adams could possibly play against the 49ers in Week 14 or maybe even the Cowboys in Week 15, but the outlook isn’t very encouraging for this coming week against the Chiefs. In the meantime, the Rams will keep leaning on Konata Mumpfield, CJ Daniels and others.“

Rams poach tight end from 49ers’ practice squad (ninersnation)

“The Los Angeles Rams are signing tight end Jack Stoll off the San Francisco 49ers’ practice squad, per NFL Network’s Mike Garafolo.

Stoll was with the Eagles from 2021 through 2024, before starting four games with the Saints last season. He had six receptions for 46 yards with New Orleans last year. For his career, the 6’4”, 247-pounder has 28 catches for 239 yards.“

Rams steal journeyman TE off 49ers’ practice squad (clutchpoints)

“The Rams are signing TE Jack Stoll off the (San Francisco) 49ers’ practice squad. With Tyler Higbee (chest) and Davis Allen (ankle) injured, Sean McVay & Co. bring in the veteran Stoll as part of the mix,” wrote Garafolo on X.

The Rams acquired an experienced option to try to stem the tide while Higbee and Allen are out. Stoll is not exactly a household name, but he could be a good fit for McVay’s three-tight-end approach.

Last season, Stoll played 15 games for the New Orleans Saints, tallying six receptions for 46 yards and one touchdown.“

Tennessee could have a terrifying new weapon in 2027 thanks to the Los Angeles Rams that SEC defenses won’t see coming (atozsports)

“Josh Heupel sought advice from the Los Angeles Rams last offseason, and he should again this offseason

Heupel and the Vols’ offensive staff spent time last offseason learning from the Los Angeles Rams and the Seattle Seahawks — according to comments made by ESPN’s Cole Cubelic during Tennessee’s win over Kennesaw State earlier this season — in an effort to improve Tennessee’s quick passing game.“

item.title: Jaguars vs. Titans: Staff roundtable and game picks for Week 12
item.description: Big Cat Country previews the Jaguars’ Week 12 matchup against the Titans.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Big Cat Country’s staff roundtable!

This week, we’re previewing the Jacksonville Jaguars’ matchup against the Tennessee Titans in Week 12.

Question 1: What’s your top question about the Jaguars this week?

Travis Holmes: Following Sunday’s performance from the offensive line, the offensive struggles up front are becoming somewhat concerning. An inability to slow the opposing pass rush or establish the run has been a primary common denominator in Jacksonville’s losses to Denver and New York, as well as its near-loss to Philadelphia. The formula for defeat seems simple: keep Jacksonville’s offense in low-scoring games by dominating the offensive line and give yourselves a chance at an upset. What’s particularly concerning heading into this week is that Jacksonville currently has six offensive linemen dealing with injuries. Left tackle Walker Little and center Robert Hainsey both exited Sunday’s game and were limited in Wednesday’s practice. Jonah Monheim and Cole Van Lanen were also listed on the injury report, while Anton Harrison remains on season-ending IR. Patrick Mekari, whose 21-day window was opened on Wednesday, was also limited. He could still be a week or more away from returning. With so many moving pieces up front, the health and consistency of this unit could become a major factor on Sunday.

Gus Logue: Can Trevor Lawrence bounce back after his worst performance of the season? Liam Coen said on Friday that he’s looking for his quarterback to “get back to the basics, the details of our reads, your feet, rhythm, timing, throwing to the open guy, and just going through your progression … trust the guys to make plays, trust the protection and scheme.” The Jaguars should win this matchup because they have better players and better coaching, but in the grand scheme of things, it’d be great to see Lawrence rediscover his mojo.

Henry Zimmer: My big question is with the offensive line. Injuries are mounting up at both tackle positions and that clearly caused issues on Sunday. If the team cannot protect Trevor Lawrence, we all see what can happen. This unit needs to figure it out if the Jags are to have a shot at winning in the playoffs.

Question 2: What’s the key to a Jaguars victory this week?

Travis: The key for Jacksonville against Tennessee is getting off to a fast start on both sides of the ball. While the objective was similar in the Jaguars’ Week 10 matchup against the Titans, and the final score reflected a 17-point blowout victory, the game was much closer than the scoreboard suggested late in the game. At 8:21 remaining in the fourth quarter, Jacksonville held just a seven-point lead, leaving the offense in a position where it still needed to close the game out due to defensive struggles. Given the Jacksonville defense’s recent history of struggling to stop opponents late in games, the Jaguars would be wise to avoid allowing this matchup to become another close affair in the fourth. A strong start, coupled with consistent execution throughout the game, could go a long way toward putting Tennessee away early.

Gus: Shutting down Tennessee’s running game. Derrick Henry may not be there anymore, but the Titans did rush for 105 yards on 17 total attempts (including QB runs) two weeks ago in Nashville. Jordan Davis and Jessie Bates III will provide reinforcements for the Jaguars’ defense, which should allow Anthony Campanile to stop the run from light boxes the way he did when DaVon Hamilton was healthy. This will be a good test for Davis especially.

Henry: The key to winning is as simple as it normally is when playing far inferior teams: just play normal football and stick to the basics. Tennessee is clearly better than its record suggests but that doesn’t mean that they should be in this football game. Attack Cam Ward, run the ball, and get out with a much-needed AFC South victory. 

Question 3: Who will be an X-factor for the Jaguars this week?

Travis: My biggest question heading into this matchup revolves around the ground game, but not necessarily involving the running backs. This week’s X-factor is Tennessee Titans quarterback Cam Ward, and the use of his legs. The second-year quarterback rushed for 39 yards in the previous meeting, and Jacksonville is coming off a game in which Giants quarterback JJ McCarthy similarly rushed for 33 yards, consistently extending plays and moving the chains with his legs. If Jacksonville can correct this recent deficiency and do a better job rushing with lane integrity, it could significantly limit Tennessee’s ability to sustain drives and keep its offense behind the sticks. That adjustment could go a long way toward helping the Jaguars leave EverBank Stadium with their eighth win on Sunday.

Gus: I gotta go with Josh Cameron. The rookie receiver had his best performance of the season in Nashville (3 catches, 67 yards, 1 TD). Now that Parker Washington is week-to-week with a shoulder injury, Cameron is in line for the biggest workload of his young career. Expect him to be utilized out of the slot and in 3-TE personnel packages. I think we could be in for a very productive game for Cameron on Sunday.

Henry: Going back to my big question, I think the X-Factor this week is either Wyatt Milum or Cole Van Lanen. Which one of these guys shows up and plays well if Walker Little cannot go? In many respects, the season hangs on their shoulders if they are the two last lines of defense at the tackle position.

Final score prediction?

Travis: Jaguars 45, Titans 27

Gus: Jaguars 20, Titans 10

Henry: Jaguars 28, Titans 17

item.title: Texans Playoff Odds at Stake against Baltimore Ravens
item.description: Houston odds to make the playoffs hinge on the result of Sunday’s game
item.content:encoded:
It’s been said multiple against multiple opponents this season, but the game against the Baltimore Ravens is, and always has been, a “must win” contest for the Houston Texans. The odds are not in Houston’s favor either way, but Sunday’s game against the listless Ravens is a do-or-die scenario for the team… and potentially offensive coordinator Nick Caley.

Houston (4-6) will be without Keylan Rutledge (neck), Kayshon Boutte (hip), Brevin Jordan (foot), and Danielle Hunter (hamstring), but will have Marvin Harrison Jr. (hamstring) back in the lineup on offense. The Ravens on the other hand are dealing with critical injuries across the board. Rookie first-rounder OG Vega Ioane, DT Nnamdi Madibuike, S Jaylinn Hawkins will be out. That’s two starters and a key backup added to the list of players out for Baltimore with includes QB Lamar Jackson, OC Ethan Pocic, CB Bilhal Kone,

The rash of injuries on offense combined with a new offensive coordinator, new line coach, and new play caller. According to Yahoo Sports, the Ravens. have played five different centers and four right guards this season. Even with the injuries, the Ravens still possess some of the leagues best veteran talent. OT Ronnie Stanley, Mark Andrews, Ray Flowers, and Derek Henry are talented enough to beat any team. While they’re limited by Jacoby Brissett’s arm and ability to run the offense, the will still press the Texans defense to its limit.

The New York Times NFL Playoff Simulator projects the Texans with a 34% chance to make the playoffs with a win, but only an 11% chance if they lose. A seventh loss and fourth at home would all but seal the deal on the Texans making the playoffs.

With wins against the Ravens and the Pittsburgh Steelers in back-to-back weekends, the Texans will .500 for the first time this season and hold a 52% chance to make the playoffs according to the New York Times. The biggest matchup of the game with be Ravens’ RT Roger Rosengarten against Will Anderson Jr. WAJ will line up against the veteran RT who is having a difficult season, rated as the 57th/70 tackles according to PFF. With the carousel of players in the Ravens interior line, look for WAJ to line up on the interior on true pass rush plays.

The other two important games this week are the Patriots vs Chargers and Raiders vs. Browns.

If both the Chargers and Raiders win, Houston’s odds jump to 41% chance to make the playoffs. Houston would be tied with New England for eighth in the AFC and one game behind the Browns for the seventh and final playoff spot.

Houston is hoping they can protect Stroud against the Ravens weakened pass rush. Trey Hendrickson is having a horrible season after signing a mega-deal to leave Cincinnati. Second-round DE Zion Young has yet to record a sack. Their pass rush is lead by Mike Green, last year’s second round pick who is having a breakout season.

Have the Ravens lost six straight? Yes. Will this be an easy victory for the Texans? No. I don’t assume Houston will possess much of a home field advantage on the Sunday after Thanksgiving. Houston is looking for its second two-win streak of the season and need to capitalize on a wounded bird to kickstart their campaign for the playoffs. According to NYT and pure logic, this Ravens game is critical to the Texans getting back on schedule. A win against an AFC opponent with a similar record will boost the Texans chances and get the team back on track to keep their three-year playoff appearance streak alive.

item.title: Steelers WR DK Metcalf reportedly fined $26,867 for incidents that led to Week 11 ejection vs. Eagles
item.description: Metcalf attempted to poke Eagles' cornerback Cooper DeJean in the eye.
item.content:encoded:
Pittsburgh Steelers wide receiver DK Metcalf was reportedly fined twice by the NFL for a pair of incidents during last week's game against the Philadelphia Eagles that led to his ejection.

According to The Ringer's Tom Pelissero, Metcalf was fined a total of $26,867 for grabbing Cooper DeJean's facemask ($11,941) and then attempting to poke the Eagles cornerback in the eye ($14,926).

Metcalf will reportedly not face further discipline and will not appeal the fines.

In the third quarter of Pittsburgh's 19-16 loss, Metcalf was ejected after picking up his second personal foul of the game.

DK Metcalf has been ejected for unsportsmanlike conduct.

Metcalf was ejected after two personal fouls.

(📺 CBS) pic.twitter.com/f1OE50Fn6I

— NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) November 22, 2026

According to Steelers coach Mike McCarthy, a referee told him that Metcalf "poked a defender in the eye." The wide receiver denied doing that while meeting with reporters on Monday.

"I didn't try to poke him in the eye," Metcalf said. "I was just telling him to stop pushing me. That's all I said."

DeJean said after the game that Metcalf "just missed" poking him in the eye.

"Almost, almost," DeJean said. "He just missed. … We were just competing. Things like that happen in football.

"It wasn't anything crazy. Nobody was really saying anything, two guys were going at it. He was trying to block me, I was trying to get him off me. Things like that. Obviously it carried over to whatever that was at the end."

Alleged eye pokes are nothing new for Metcalf. He was fined $12,172 after Week 8 last season for sticking a finger inside the facemask of Green Bay Packers linebacker Quay Walker.

Metcalf recorded only one reception for 2 yards during that loss to the Eagles. He bounced back on Friday during a 27-5 win over the Denver Broncos, catching three balls for 36 yards and a touchdown.
