item.title: Previewing the New York Jets’ opposition: Miami Dolphins
item.description: The Jets take on the Miami Dolphins in Miami this Sunday
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins haven’t lost to the Jets in Miami since 2014. That was the game when Geno Smith, in his first stint with the Jets, lit them up in a 37-24 win, posting a perfect quarterback rating. The Jets will be favored to end the drought on Sunday against the 1-9 Dolphins, even though Miami beat them 28-25 last month at MetLife Stadium.

Let’s break down the Dolphins’ roster going position by position:

Quarterbacks

A lot has changed since these teams met four weeks ago. The most significant change being that quarterback Malik Willis is now on injured reserve.

This means that the current starter is Kyle McCord, who until two weeks ago had never thrown an NFL pass.

McCord didn’t disgrace himself in his first game, which was a close loss to the struggling Colts. He ended up with just over 200 yards and a rushing touchdown as he completed 17 of 32 passes.

He didn’t fare so well against the Bills on Sunday, though, as he barely reached 100 passing yards, completing only 12 of 32 passes.

The backup to McCord is a familiar face – Brady Cook, who started over the last month of the season for the Jets as an undrafted rookie in 2025.

Offensive Line

On the offensive line, the starting group has stayed healthy, with center Aaron Brewer and rookie left guard Kaydn Proctor missing one start each and the other three starters having played all year.

A change has been discussed, though, as right tackle Austin Jackson has given up a team-high five sacks and could be replaced there by Proctor at some point. This move would be made with an eye on the future, as Jackson is out of contract at the end of the year and the first round pick Proctor has had a good year inside, but did play tackle in college.

Left tackle Patrick Paul has had a decent year despite giving up a team-high seven penalties, but right guard Jonah Savaiinaea continues to be a weak link.

The backups include center Andrew Meyer and guard Jarrett Kingston, who have started one game each this year. Sixth round rookie DJ Campbell was recently released to the practice squad after the team claimed Christian Haynes from Seattle.

Chukwuebuka Godrick and Caedan Wallace round out this group.

Running Backs

After De’Von Achane was lost for the year, Ollie Gordon II has settled in as the number one back and it’s not out of the question he could make a run at a thousand-yard season as he’s already got over 600 rushing yards at 4.4 per carry and racked up over 100 in the last meeting against the Jets.

Backup Jaylen Wright has been staggeringly inefficient in reserve, as he has just 49 yards on 30 carries. The number three, rookie Kaytron Allen, has just two carries for minus-one yard, but did catch a 46-yard pass.

DJ Herman remains on the roster as a blocking back.

Pass catchers

Miami’s reloaded pass catching group got a boost in the last meeting between these teams as third round rookie Caleb Douglas returned from injury to catch two decisive touchdown passes.

The Dolphins’ leading receiver is Malik Washington, but he has just eight catches for 101 yards over the past three games.

Tight end Greg Dulcich has been the other main contributor with 26 catches and his 86 yards on five catches against the Jets easily represents his best output of the season.

Miami will be hoping for more over the rest of the season from their other rookie pass catchers. Chris Bell, a third round pick, has good size at wide receiver but just 13 catches. Fifth rounder Kevin Coleman has just nine receptions, although two were for a touchdown. They also have three rookie tight ends backing up Dulcich – Will Kacmarek was selected in the third round and Seydou Traore in the fifth, while Justin Joly was picked up from Denver, who also drafted him in the fifth round.

Additional depth at wideout comes from Jalen Tolbert but Jared Wayne has been ruled out.

Defensive Line

The biggest change on defense since these teams last met is that defensive lineman Zach Sieler, arguably their best remaining veteran player, is now on injured reserve. In addition, the other two starters – Zeek Biggers and Jordan Phillips – were also placed on injured reserve.

This leaves former first round pick Kenneth Grant, who himself had only recently returned from injury, as a starter alongside Keith Cooper Jr., who was poached from the Panthers’ practice squad a couple of weeks ago.

Jordan Jefferson was recently signed from the practice squad and was the main backup last week.

Ex-Jet Eric Watts, who as we know can also play on the edge, was also signed to the main roster from the practice squad and was the fourth man in the interior rotation last week.

On the edge, Chop Robinson has recently picked things up after a slow start. He has five sacks to lead the team, including four in the past five games.

Josh Uche has three sacks as the other starter on the edge with Malik Herring as the main backup and undrafted rookie Rodney McGraw behind him. Robert Beal Jr. was recently released.

Linebackers

Second round pick Jacob Rodriguez has continued to impress at linebacker with 93 tackles and two interceptions, although last year’s leading tackler, Jordyn Brooks, is right behind him with 92 tackles.

Willie Gay also plays a role in base packages, but Jackson Woodard is primarily just a special teamer.

Following Shaka Heyward’s recent release, Miami has just four linebackers on the active roster as fourth round pick Trey Moore remains on injured reserve. However, veteran Ronnie Harrison was himself just activated from injured reserve and his game status for Sunday is questionable.

Defensive Backs

Miami has recently got some guys back in the secondary, with rookie safety Kyle Louis having returned from injured reserve and Darrell Baker Jr. having been activated from the PUP list.

Both are currently in rotational roles, though, as fifth round rookie Michael Taaffe and Dante Trader as still listed as the starting safeties with Jason Marshall and JuJu Brents outside and first round pick Chris Johnson in the slot.

On Sunday, Trader missed the game due to injury and Zayne Anderson started in his place. Trader should be available to play this weekend but Brents, who has a team-high seven penalties, has been ruled out.

Safety Julius Wood and ex-Jet Jaylin Simpson are the only other Dolphins defensive backs to see action this year, albeit only 30 snaps between them. Cornerback Marcellas Dial is also on the roster.

Special Teams

The Dolphins are currently on their third kicker as Daniel Carlson recently took over from Zane Gonzalez. Carlson is currently being elevated from the practice squad each week. He made three of three field goals in his Miami debut last week.

At punter, the situation is also clouded by the fact that Bradley Pinion isn’t 100 percent. The Dolphins signed Jack Browning to the active roster as well as cover and he will punt this weekend as Pinion has been ruled out.

In the return game, Washington has been handling punts and Wright has been doing most of the kickoff returning. Coleman has also been involved.

Simpson is the primary gunner and has been productive in kick coverage, as have Louis and Woodard.

item.title: Stock up, stock down: Bears shock Lions on Thanksgiving
item.description: After a wild comeback win, @SamHouseholder has his weekly stock watch.
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Bears have nine wins and have clinched consecutive winning seasons for the first time since 2005 and 2006.

And they took the lead in the division.

It was the first time this season the Bears had to dip into their 2025 bag for one of their late-game heroic comebacks.

No complaints, of course; getting the W was the most important thing and there are no style points in the NFL.

Since most of this season has been winning from taking an early lead, watching the Bears come from behind felt oddly nostalgic.

It was definitely stressful, though.

I was relieved when the Bears won, so I wouldn’t be in an awful mood for the rest of the holiday.

Let’s get to this week’s stock watch.

Stock up

Dillon Thieneman, S – I’ve already committed the correct spelling of Thieneman to memory, which is a good sign. He was second on the team in tackles. His interception came at the exact right time when the team needed it. He now has three interceptions this season, which leads the Bears.

T.J. Edwards, LB – Anytime you think Edwards’ best is behind him, he comes up clutch. He’s made some fantastic plays in key moments this year. And perhaps none were bigger than Thursday’s tackles of Sam LaPorta on third down and then coming right back and tackling Jahmyr Gibbs. Gibbs has been perhaps the toughest player to tackle this season. Plus, he tipped the pass that Thieneman ended up intercepting.

Rome Odunze, WR – Odunze always seems to come up clutch for the Bears and his QB. His 41-yard touchdown saved the game. Then his spectacular toe-tap catch in the corner of the endzone won the game. The game-winner also came on a fantastic route. Rome has hit another level over the last month and he and Burden are going to be an even bigger part of the pass game without Cole Kmet and Colston Loveland.

Stock down

Montez Sweat, DE – You can take your pick for the DL here, but I’m singling out Sweat. The Bears had zero sacks. Credit goes to the Lions, for sure. You could see the extra attention they gave to Jeffery Simmons. But Sweat was credited with just two tackles. It was a poor showing for the defensive line that’s been greatly improved since Simmons’ arrival.

Theo Benedet, LT – Theo has been mostly good this season, but he struggled against the Lions. A lot of the pressure Caleb had came from the left side or up the middle. We all know what Bradbury is, but Benedet takes the spot this week.

Malik Muhammad, CB – It wasn’t all bad, but his run support had a couple of bad moments. And while the Bears’ defense as a whole had its share of moments against Jahmyr Gibbs, one of the best in football, it was Muhammad who I saw missing opportunities the most against Detroit.

Who is on your up and down lists this week? Who do you think performed great and not-so-great against Detroit?

item.title: Mike McCarthy admits he neglected key Steelers area after Aaron Rodgers criticism
item.description: Mike McCarthy appears to have done some self-reflection amid the Aaron Rodgers firestorm.
item.content:encoded:
Mike McCarthy appears to have done some self-reflection amid the Aaron Rodgers firestorm. 

The Steelers coach admitted he neglected the team’s defense a little too much during his first season with the team following a 27-5 throttling of the Broncos at Acrisure Stadium on Black Friday. 

“I have not spent enough time with the defense,” McCarthy told reporters after the win. “You know, and that’s something that, as far as job responsibility, job description, you know, these are things that’ll be looked at in the offseason. But, you know, it’s a point in our year where we’re making adjustments and definitely conscientious of it. 

“But at the end of the day, we have to all do our jobs and make sure we’re giving the players the plan and all the other things that they need that we can perform and play with that type of urgency, physicality that we played today.”

Rodgers, who was benched late Tuesday night and released by the team on Wednesday, was critical of McCarthy, an offensive coach, during his appearance on “The Pat McAfee Show” on Wednesday for not forging enough of a relationship with the team’s defense players

“There were some guys early on that were … didn’t like the way things were going, especially defensive guys. Mike didn’t want to get to know the defense,” Rodgers claimed. “At one point, I told him, ‘You should really lean into the defensive guys a little bit more and talk to those guys,’ and he said, ‘Well, I don’t think I need to.’ And I said, ‘Well, I disagree with that.’ He already kind of lost a lot of those guys.”

Rodgers was heavily critical of McCarthy during his appearance on the McAfee show, accusing him of missing offensive meetings, falling asleep in them and being behind on film work by his standards.

Follow the Post’s coverage of Aaron Rodgers’ release from the Pittsburgh Steelers:

  • Aaron Rodgers calls out Tom Brady for comments on locker room ‘sanctity’
  • Aaron Rodgers-less Steelers end chaotic week with resounding win over Broncos
  • Aaron Rodgers claims he was ‘barred’ from Steelers facility in shocking text to Al Michaels
  • Aaron Rodgers became the very thing he railed against the Jets for

It led to Rodgers presenting an ultimatum to the coach he won a Super Bowl with in 2011 with the Packers. The QB asked McCarthy to give up the playcalling duties 

McCarthy was initially open to the change as Rodgers was calling plays himself in recent weeks, but was advised not to by “some in the locker room,” according to Netflix NFL insider Tom Pelissero.

He ultimately decided to call Rodgers on it and start Rudolph instead of him. 

“We got to a point, we talked some things — you know communication and things like that — and there was an ultimatum made clearly outside of his job description and so it was my decision to bench him,” McCarthy told reporters on Wednesday.

Rodgers is currently a free agent after clearing waivers and can sign with any NFL team.

Rodgers has been highly criticized by the Steelers owner Art Rooney, former teammates, NFL stars and media members for going public with what occurred in the Steelers building. Fox play-by-play man and seven-time Super Bowl champion Tom Brady called Rodgers out for breaking “the sanctity of an NFL locker room.”

Rodgers responded to Brady with a text to Amazon’s play-by-play voice Al Michaels that claimed he was “barred” from the Pittsburgh facility after being benched. 

“A lot of talk about the sanctity of the locker room, [Rodgers] said, ‘The code of sanctity exists to protect the integrity of the locker room, not to provide immunity from accountability for its leadership,’” Michaels said.

The Steelers defense looked just fine on a rainy Friday as Broncos quarterback Bo Nix went 22-of-49 passing for 169 yards and was sacked three times.

He was also forced into three turnovers, including a first-quarter fumble recovered for a touchdown.

item.title: Week 12 NFL picks against the spread, predictions for every game: Can the Seahawks, or anyone, stop the 49ers?
item.description: The 49ers have one win over the Seahawks already, and are looking for another.
item.content:encoded:
Last season, the San Francisco 49ers won a close game at the Seattle Seahawks. And then after that the Seahawks became a dominant Super Bowl champion, including two blowout wins of the 49ers.

We have the 49ers' road win over the Seahawks out of the way already this season. But this season San Francisco is the team that looks like a future Super Bowl champion.

The 49ers have been great this season, including a dominant win over the Minnesota Vikings last week. The offense has been spectacular. And the defense, ranked seventh in DVOA, has been one of the biggest surprises of the season. That defense has brought the 49ers from being a good team to a potentially great one. Kyle Shanahan, who should be NFL Coach of the Year, was going to field a potent offense. The defense completes the circle.

However, we can't count out the Seahawks quite yet. The defense has been tremendous again. The offense hasn't been great, but a lot of that is attributed to Sam Darnold playing through injuries almost all season, when he has been able to play. Darnold should return this week, off the Seahawks' bye, and if he's a little healthier and a bit more protective of the ball, Seattle can still play at a high level.

That's why the Seahawks are not a big underdog this week, even though they play at a 9-1 49ers team. The 49ers are just a 3-point favorite. Not setting the spread above a field goal shows a lot of respect for the reigning champions. But maybe it's not showing enough respect for the 49ers.

San Francisco has shown no signs of vulnerability. It had no issues with the Vikings defense, which is the only defense on the same level as Seattle. This looks like a great San Francisco team, and that's why 49ers -3 is the pick. And if the Seahawks can't slow down the 49ers, nobody else in the NFC might be able to do it either.

Here are the rest of the picks against the spread for Week 12 of the NFL season:

Bengals (-10) over Saints

The Bengals should be upset after losing in the final seconds at Washington on Monday night. And they can take it out on the Saints, who have lost three of four with the only win being when they held off an overtime two-point conversation at home against Shedeur Sanders and the Browns. Joe Burrow should have another monster game.

Jets (-3.5) over Dolphins

Kyle McCord was reasonable in his first start, but that was against the Colts. Last week at Buffalo the Dolphins had what was probably their worst game of the season, and that's saying something for a 1-9 team. The Jets aren't good, but they are coming off a win over the Chargers, and they'll look better when they're playing teams down at their level.

Texans (-7) over Ravens

The worst thing to happen to Jesse Minter is the defense struggling as badly as it has. If the Ravens were losing because the offense was inept without Lamar Jackson, it would be easy to give him a pass. But Jacoby Brissett has been reasonable and the defense, which is Minter's specialty, has been awful. Baltimore has allowed 32.4 points per game over the past five weeks. The Texans can move the ball and now see an opening for a wild-card spot with the upheaval in Pittsburgh.

Falcons (+7) over Vikings

It's hard to take any underdog lately, with the favorites on a roll the past few weeks. And the Falcons aren't a comfortable underdog to take, but Atlanta has enough talent that it's still the only team to beat the 49ers. The Falcons are coming off a bye, and maybe that helps them keep it close.

Colts (+6.5) over Giants

Switching quarterbacks can give a team a short-term boost, especially when that quarterback was the worst in the NFL this season. Daniel Jones wasn't giving the Colts a chance. Anthony Richardson Sr. hasn't been good in the NFL, but he can't be worse than Jones has been. Maybe there's a jolt that gives Indianapolis a chance to keep this one close.

Titans (+14.5) over Jaguars

It would have been nice to see the Titans play better at Dallas last week, but they did end up scoring 30 points. The offense has been decent lately. The problem is the defense, and that's why it's scary to take them even getting more than two touchdowns. But that's a big spread in the NFL.

Patriots (+1.5) over Chargers

This game could be Tommy DeVito vs. D.J. Uiagalelei, if Justin Herbert doesn't clear concussion protocol. Since there's no reason to rush Herbert back we'll assume he won't play, and then this could turn into one of the ugliest games in the NFL this season.

Commanders (-7) over Cardinals

The Cardinals have shown no signs of life lately, after trading Jacoby Brissett, watching Gardner Minshew II go down to injury, losing all their receivers due to injury or trades and then firing their defensive coordinator this week. Whether rookie Carson Beck returns from a back injury or Josh Johnson has to start again, it doesn't really matter. The Commanders aren't great but we can't trust Arizona.

Raiders (+4.5) over Browns

Fernando Mendoza didn't look bad last week. The Raiders' defense is still terrible and maybe the Browns break out against it, but Cleveland's offense has its issues too. The Browns play close games, that's what they do, and we'll assume another close one on Sunday night.

Buccaneers (-3) over Panthers

Tampa Bay is getting very little out of Baker Mayfield. But the Buccaneers can still run the ball and play very good defense. A win for Tampa Bay would still leave them at 4-7, but they'd be just a game behind the Panthers for first place and clinch the head-to-head tiebreaker. The first meeting was an absolute blowout, and while that won't repeat, it showed that Tampa Bay is a hard matchup for Carolina.

This week: 4-0-1

Last week: 2-11

Season to date: 74-92-3

item.title: Miami Dolphins offensive line review: Tracking the guards in Week 11
item.description: A weekly scorecard tracking the development of Dolphin guards Kadyn Proctor and Jonah Savaiinaea.
item.content:encoded:
Folks, this was not a good game on offense. For one, it was the sixth time this season the Dolphins were held under 14 points, leaving them last in the NFL in scoring. For another, Kyle McCord completed just 12 of 33 passes for 86 net yards. The offensive line was far from solely responsible for the struggles, but it certainly didn’t help matters.

Still, rookie left guard Kadyn Proctor and second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea remain key pieces of the Dolphins’ future. Each week, we take a closer look at Proctor and Savaiinaea and examine what analysts are saying about their most recent performances.

Kadyn Proctor

Jonah Savaiinaea

What We Learned

The game against the Bills showed a lot of the same problems we’ve seen the last few weeks. Austin Jackson (PFF grade: an offense-worst 34.6!) put up very little resistance against Bills defensive lineman Greg Rousseau, who logged two sacks of Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord. McCord also continued to hold the ball for too long, and the team’s pass catchers need to keep working on their blocking.

Kadyn Proctor, fresh off of one of his best games this season against the Colts (by PFF standards), had his worst against the Bills (by PFF standards). While he didn’t give up any sacks, he did allow 1 quarterback hit, 3 hurries and 4 pressures. His issues appeared to stem largely from rookie mistakes: hesitation, slow recognition when helping teammates and getting caught by Deone Walker’s swim move. That said, in taking a spin around Dolphins analysts looking at the offensive line, most either viewed Proctor’s performance as adequate or spent more time debating whether he should finish the season at right tackle (more on that later).

The same was true for Jonah Savaiinaea, but in reverse. By PFF standards, his performances against the Bills and Colts were his best since Week 2, and he also allowed only 1 pressure and 1 hurry, with no QB hits or sacks. Still, there were a fair amount of mistakes that need to be cleaned up. He still had his share of losing reps, including several against Deone Walker, and at one point he and Austin Jackson opened up a huge running lane for a defensive tackle to record a tackle for loss. I’m hopeful that six weeks of Savaiinaea’s well-below-average play is obscuring his more recent only-below-average play, and he can keep turning around his on-field reputation. It’s worth mentioning that Savaiinaea missed a few plays at the end of the first half due to an ankle injury, but he played the entire second half.

As to the “Proctor playing right tackle” question, it’s worth mentioning that Mel Kiper (whose reputation these days feels on par with PFF’s) labels guard and tackle among the weakest in the 2027 draft. Maybe that’s an argument for moving Proctor outside. Then again, given how difficult it has been to find quality guard play, I could be convinced the Dolphins should leave well enough alone.

The tracker will be updated each week throughout the season. For a more in-depth breakdown of Proctor’s and Savaiinaea’s performance, check out offensive line Coach Eric Smith’s film analysis of the game, which you can find on his YouTube channel, Focused on Fins.

Towards the end of the Kansas City Chiefs’ 13-10 loss to the Buffalo Bills, a tough catch over the middle by wide receiver Rashee Rice appeared to keep the Chiefs alive late. However, further review overturned the ruling on the field, and many in Chiefs Kingdom have their gripes about it.

The latest Kansas City Chiefs news

Rashee Rice, Chiefs believe he caught pivotal 3rd-down pass late vs. Bills | ESPN

“Yes, I did,” Rice said with a blank expression when asked if he believed he made the reception.

Instead, Rice said none of the officials explained to him why his 11-yard catch on third-and-10 from the Chiefs’ 9-yard line was overturned into an incompletion after a replay review was conducted by the NFL’s headquarters in New York City. The play ended with Rice attempting to make a contented catch in the middle of the field after he was hit, while in the air, by Bills safety Amani Hooker.

A few minutes later, the Bills and their fans inside Highmark Stadium cheered when referee Alex Kemp announced that the pass from quarterback Patrick Mahomes was incomplete because the ball, while in Rice’s right hand, hit the turf.

“We were first told that they were reviewing the spot, so I didn’t even know that we were reviewing the catch,” Mahomes said. “From my angle, when I threw the ball, I thought his hand was under the ball.”

Brittany Mahomes Slams “Joke” Call From Controversial Kansas City Chiefs, Buffalo Bills Thanksgiving Game | E! News

“HAHAHAHAHAHA WHAT A JOKE,” Brittany posted to her Instagram Stories Nov. 26. “Guess we can’t even play football without getting it called against us.”

The 31-year-old—who is expecting her fourth child with the Chiefs quarterback—added, “Not sure what an actual catch is after that | guess? I don’t wanna hear s–t anymore from anyone.”

Questions emerge about how the Chiefs ran a 1-second play late in loss to Bills | The Kansas City Star

Another strange sequence took place on the Chiefs’ final drive of the game. This is from the gamebook.

1-10-KC 11 (:26) (Shotgun) P.Mahomes FUMBLES (Aborted) at KC 7, and recovers at KC 6.

Timeout #1 by BUF at 00:25.

2-15-KC 6 (:25) (Shotgun) E.Johnson right guard to KC 11 for 5 yards (B.Chubb; G.Rousseau).

That fumble by Mahomes took just 1 second off the clock, and that left fans with questions about how that was even possible.

The Good News About the Chiefs After Thanksgiving Heartbreaker in Buffalo | Sports Illustrated

Still, even if we take the most aggressive worst-case path forward for Kansas City in the next several weeks, they’re still a playoff team.

Get pessimistic and say the Chiefs lose to the Rams, Bengals, and 49ers, while beating the Patriots, Chargers and Raiders. That would leave Kansas City with an 11-6 record—probably good enough for the No. 5 or 6 seed in the AFC, but certainly a playoff spot. Throw in an upset loss to the Tommy DeVito-led Patriots (which I do not think will happen, to be clear) and they’re 10-7, still punching a ticket to the playoffs.

Around the NFL

Steelers dominate Broncos days after releasing Aaron Rodgers as Bo Nix struggles | The Athletic

T.J. Watt’s first-quarter touchdown off a strip-sack got the scoring started, and Jalen Ramsey’s 36-yard pick-six with 1:33 left in the first half provided more than enough cushion. DK Metcalf also bounced back after last week’s ejection, scoring a touchdown on a 22-yard pass from Rudolph.

The loss snapped a six-game winning streak for the Broncos, who missed an opportunity to get separation from the Kansas City Chiefs atop the AFC West. They also fell two games behind the Buffalo Bills in the race for the AFC’s top playoff seed. Quarterback Bo Nix struggled, with his two first-half turnovers putting the Broncos in a big hole, and a fourth-quarter, fourth-down interception ending any hopes of a comeback on a rainy day in Pittsburgh. The Broncos fell to 8-3 and host the Miami Dolphins in Week 13.

Aaron Rodgers releases new statement via Al Michaels, says he went on ‘Pat McAfee Show’ after Steelers barred him from team facility | Yahoo! Sports

As for how things played out with the Steelers, it’s known that Rodgers made some sort of ultimatum — reportedly that he wanted to call plays on offense or be released — and the Steelers opted to announce his benching late Tuesday night and then release him Wednesday after he aired his grievances against McCarthy.

Rodgers claimed he got no communication from McCarthy until his benching was announced, and that he only appeared on McAfee’s show after the Steelers barred him from their facility:

“They took this public, never heard from the head coach, then they leak at 11:00 p.m. They also barred me from the facility. That’s why I went to McAfee.”

NFL Week 12 injury report: Brock Purdy, Justin Herbert out as QB health dwindles across league | CBS Sports

The San Francisco 49ers will be without an MVP contender on Sunday as Brock Purdy deals with an ankle injury that occurred in last week’s win over the Minnesota Vikings. Coach Kyle Shanahan said this week that it is not a high ankle sprain, which is good news, but he did not practice at all in the lead-up to the NFC West battle against the Seattle Seahawks. Mac Jones, who is widely regarded as a top-flight backup, is in line to make his first start of the year.

And in Southern California, an already dismal Los Angeles Chargers offense could become even more ineffective with Justin Herbert ruled out for the contest against the New England Patriots. The worst offense in the league by EPA per play is poised to insert DJ Uiagalelei into action for the first start of his career.

item.title: Cowboys vs. Eagles Stock Report: Brian Schottenheimer finds a new low
item.description: The Cowboys continue to find new lows
item.content:encoded:
It is often said that when people continue to show and tell you who they are, you should believe them.

The Dallas Cowboys have done a ton of showing, a ton of telling, and here we sit with no choice. We must believe that they are not only not a good football team, but they are a fundamentally bad football team with no point of optimism in sight.

Admissions like this are sobering from a fan perspective. There will be people who read what I just wrote and say that they have known this for a long time. They didn’t need more showing. More telling was unnecessary. They have known.

That may be true. But it doesn’t change how disappointing, frustrating, and saddening it is that the Cowboys insist on declaring that this is life rooting for them these days.

Thanksgiving Day was an abomination. Our stock report reflects that pretty clearly.

Stock Down: Brian Schottenheimer

It has often been said/joked that it is silly to keep including Schottenheimer here as it is hard to imagine how his stock could be lower. What we just saw should serve as a lesson that when you toss out that challenge, he will find a way.

Since the loss it has been shared a ton on social media that NFL teams are 72-0-1 when leading by at least 14 points in the fourth quarter this season. The Cowboys are now 3-2. Think about that.

As noted, we don’t really need to say more. This team has a lot of issues. To be fair to Schottenheimer, they had many of those issues before he ever even worked for them in any capacity. But right now he is the problem that needs the most stern levels of addressing.

Stock Down: Jerry Jones

Again, we have had this conversation before.

You aren’t wrong when you say that Jerry Jones needs to do this or that, but I imagine that you are like me in that you are exhausted from those conversations. We have been having them for literally decades now.

Jerry made this bed. Then he continued to create all of the attention around it so that when we lie in it those around us treat us like fools for believing in our favorite football team.

Rooting for this team has become a chore. That is totally on Jerry.

Stock Down: Brandon Aubrey

Should the laces have been out? Clearly there is a debate there.

But Brandon Aubrey clearly has an issue right now. We explained it away by saying his misses were only from downtown, and then he made a 59-yard field goal in this game that was noted as the longest field goal ever on Thanksgiving Day. Things were good again.

But then Aubrey missed a routine 40-yard field goal that proved costly. What’s more is that beyond just missing the field goal, Aubrey put everyone (Schottenheimer included) in a bind on the late 4th-and-1 where they couldn’t trust him.

It isn’t proper to count other people’s pockets, but Aubrey is the highest-paid kicker in the NFL. We are way past the point of understandable errors. He is an issue.

Stock Down: Cobie Durant

The interception at the end was fun, but it obviously didn’t matter.

What did matter was the damage that preceded (and followed) it. Cobie Durant was getting fully bullied by Joe Milton of all people.

We told ourselves that the Cowboys were simply dealing with injuries to the secondary, that when players like Cobie Durant returned all would calm down (relatively speaking).

Here we still are.

Stock Down: Rashan Gary

Social media hsa been pretty hard on Rashan Gary this season, and at this point I don’t know how anyone can defend him in any capacity.

On the massive Milton bomb to DeVonta Smith you could see Gary have absolutely zero awareness that a play was active. We can’t speak to what he was thinking obviously, but these types of things continue to happen with him.

I maintain that I appreciated the Cowboys pursuing veterans who they thought could help, ones who their defensive coordinator had a history with and clearly was fond of. Obviously those decisions didn’t pan out. Now I am worried that they will abandon that type of philosophy altogether moving forward.

Stock Up: KaVontae Turpin

There were clearly good points in this game before it all fell apart, and KaVontae Turpin had one of them. This is now back-to-back weeks where Turpin justified not only his roster spot, but his continued inclusion on the offensive side of the ball.

Forecasting the future on any level is difficult with this team, but Turpin is a worthy player to be on this roster. We might be nearing the end of those days as the team continues to waste things away, though.

Stock Up: Javonte Williams

We can certainly talk about all that has been wasted, more on that in a bit, and one of the under-the-radar things in that capacity is the production that Dallas has gotten from Javonte Williams since he arrived.

Thursday was another example of Williams fulfilling his obligation. I think we all would have liked to have seen him get an opportunity to do just that on the ill-fated 4th-and-1 where Dak Prescott was sacked.

Sad Stock: Dak Prescott

Speaking of.

I recognize, know, understand, and have the scars to prove that Dak Prescott is a divisive subject around here. There may be some who feel he needs to do more. I don’t know what to tell these people at this point.

The bar that I at least hope most people can clear is that Prescott is absolutely doing enough for the Cowboys to win games. This has been the case for a long time. He cannot do everything because he is just one man. We are on the verge of the Cowboys having nothing to show for his career like they do his predecessor and that is just a sad overall reality, for Prescott included.

Sad Stock: CeeDee Lamb

CeeDee Lamb is in this group for me, too. He and his quarterback are about to join the list that Romo, Jason Witten (who we may see again), Dez Bryant, Sean Lee, DeMarcus Ware (as a Cowboy), Terence Newman, Tyron Smith, Zack Martin, we could go on and on and on and on, are all a part of. The list of wasted talents.

How many players will one day see their names hang in the Ring of Honor while having never played a seirous playoff game for the franchise? That is as subjective way of looking at this, but you get my point.

What’s more is that the Cowboys are currently experiencing perhaps the best season from Lamb (Prescott on some level, too). They aren’t just wasting elite talents. They are wasting them at the peak of their powers.

Sad Stock: All of us

This post-loss thought hit me a little differently as the game was on Thanksgiving Day.

Like I’m sure is/was the case for many of you, much of my upbringing and current life on Thanksgiving Day involved the Dallas Cowboys. We talk often about how it is a unique holiday for us because our favorite team plays on it every year. The game and everything around it is woven into how we structure, plan, and ultimately celebrate the holiday.

Once upon a time the pomp and circumstance of the Cowboys of it all was such a big deal. The wins were euphoric. The losses were devastating. The emotions rode all across the roller coaster of the spectrum.

We are mad right now, perhaps even devastated on some level, but I don’t think we are upset the way we were after Thanksgiving losses of the past.

Jerry Jones said it best in his postgame comments by saying that he felt numb. I think we feel that way, too. I think that this team has been this way for so long that it is now just a thing. It isn’t the thing.

The heart, soul, and spirit of our collective fandom has withered away in my opinion. This hasn’t been the case just because of The Drought™. I think, not speaking for anyone, that we can all ultimately come to terms with losing. Dez caught it. All of that stuff.

But this team isn’t losing. This team is existing. This team is biding time. This group of people that we have assigned so much to is simply going through the motions.

And now that’s all we are doing as well.

item.title: Mike McCarthy, front office, still has plenty to prove after Week 12 win
item.description: Beating the Broncos lowers the volume, but it hasn’t fixed all the underlying problems.
item.content:encoded:
Boy, did the Steelers need that one.

After a tumultuous past couple of days that rivaled even the most contentious of family arguments taking place across America over the Thanksgiving holiday, the Pittsburgh Steelers, perhaps miraculously, emerged victorious Friday. Pittsburgh’s 27-5 victory over the Denver Broncos was the first such final score in NFL history, and yet to tenured fans of the Black and Gold, this was possibly the most typical Steelers win imaginable.

Stop me if this sounds familiar. Heading into the game, the Steelers were coming into the week on a two-game losing streak that featured an embarrassing blowout loss to a division rival and then a close loss to a sub-.500 team with questionable and/or backup quarterback play. Throw in a pinch of humiliating locker room revelations via local reporting, some palace intrigue involving a change with a key member of the offensive system, and an upcoming opponent that entered the week with one of the better records in the AFC, and you have a game that, logically, the Steelers should absolutely lose. So, of course, they win instead.

If the headlines of this past week weren’t still so fresh in all of our minds, that last paragraph reads much like the last eight years of Steelers football. Ever since Ben Roethlisberger tore his elbow up in Week 2 of the 2019 season — though some Yinzer would argue even earlier than that — that has been this organization’s MO. Believe me, I’m rolling my eyes right along with you as we once again discuss the Steelers Way of the past decade: lose some headscratchers to bad teams, gather some ugly wins just as you’ve written them off, win enough games to make the playoffs, and then promptly roll over in the Wild Card round.

Friday was a welcome result in the short term, but it did little to shake the belief that the Steelers are going through the same patterns I just outlined, and that many in the fanbase have shared in our comment sections for years.

In our weekly preview column, my colleague Ryland Bickley and I outlined that Denver’s record felt a little fraudulent compared to how they’d been performing on the field. In fact, they felt a little Steelers-ish, including quarterback Bo Nix’s play being eerily similar to that of now-ex-Steeler Aaron Rodgers. Essentially, Denver’s offense has been one of the worst in the league, and the Broncos have relied on winning close games on the back of their talented, albeit flawed, defense. Call them Pittsburgh West.

Sure enough, Bo Nix all but single-handedly handed this game to the Steelers. The quarterback playing most like 2026 Aaron Rodgers continued to do so.

On offense, the Steelers didn’t change much structurally. The concepts were generally the same, but the big differences were:

  • A clear and obvious swing back to the run in the team’s run-pass balance (31-16, 65.9% run). Still, it wasn’t that effective (3.8 YPC), if we’re being honest. This team will continue to miss Mason McCormick.
  • More under center.
  • More motion pre-snap.

Again, the win was nice. I will never root against a Steelers win. But it would be dishonest to pretend like the offense was fixed. The defense scored two touchdowns; the offense scored one. The defense put 14 points on the board; the offense 13. I’m not telling you anything groundbreaking by reminding you that the defense cannot be expected to score like that every week, especially come January.

So that brings us back to McCarthy. I won’t relitigate all the goriest gossip that came out this week — my column partner Ryland already laid it out spectacularly — but I do want to touch on what this should mean moving forward.

Realistically, do I expect Art Rooney II to can McCarthy in-season, especially after this win? Certainly not. Rooney has already come out and said the politically correct thing: that he supports his coach 100%. Heck, I fully acknowledge that the most realistic outcome is Rooney sticking by his man and letting McCarthy play out his contract or retire on his terms after another couple of seasons.

But as a lifelong fan of this team, I wish Rooney cared as much as the rest of us. Or could at least use some logic and common sense.

I don’t pretend to have all the answers, or the ability to predict the future. But this week’s embarrassment was not hard to see coming. We’d already seen a nasty breakup between Rodgers and McCarthy with the Packers, which was detailed in a 2019 tell-all article. They’re that couple you know that clearly hates each other, are always yelling at each other in public, but still tries to get back together despite the rest of the friend group’s wincing.

And just like a messy couple, we likely can’t take anything either side says at 100% face value. Still, there were certainly enough specific details about their relationship that came out to make you wonder why any franchise, let alone the quarterback and coach, would think testing a reunion could end any other way than poorly. It doesn’t all have to be true; it should have been obvious to the front office that it was a profoundly doomed idea.

We have also had years with Rodgers in the public eye to know that while he was once a great quarterback, he’s one of the league’s biggest grudge holders, a little self-absorbed at best, egomaniacal at worst, and generally a player who has been all too comfortable airing out the faults of his peers, coaches, and front office members to the media, while bristling at any critical words directed his way.

I’m sure some fans will believe he’s earned that right. They will tell me I’m just a hater in the comments. But let’s be real, I was never going to change their minds anyway. There are people who still believe Rodgers was playing well, despite mounting evidence to the contrary. Regardless, I have eyes and ears, and I know it’s possible for two things to be true at once: Rodgers can be beloved and respected by his teammates, and still ultimately be a selfish, bad teammate. How Rodgers went out isn’t the actions of a person who was trying to do the greater good for the teammates he loved, no matter how much effort he puts into framing the narrative that way. And like, Forrest Gump:


To be clear, I don’t come down on McCarthy’s “side” either. I side with wanting what’s best for the Pittsburgh Steelers.

I had concerns about hiring McCarthy this winter, not only because of that Green Bay exposé, but because McCarthy has always come across as a bit sloppy in the details, and as a person who at times is more savvy in navigating the palace intrigue of the NFL than winning the big games on the field. As I detailed in my previous article, when McCarthy was making his first comeback, he spoke about watching all the offensive film in the NFL from the previous season, just to admit he lied about it during his opening press conference.

And when it came time to answer for this week’s allegations, McCarthy has fessed up to some of it without denying anything. That’s admirable in a certain regard, but again doesn’t quiet the initial concerns I and others voiced about hiring him.

But more importantly than the he-said-he-said drama between a coach and quarterback, or even some slight fibbing during a job interview, McCarthy’s recent results speak loudly enough. He’s always been a coach good enough to win in the regular season. But when there are questions about how prepared you get your team and how sharp you are on the details, how do these facts about his last five playoff games come off:

  • In McCarthy’s last five coached playoff games (2 with GB, 3 with DAL), his teams have scored a combined 26 first-half points – an average of 5.2 points.
  • In those same five games, McCarthy’s teams were outscored 83-26, a differential of 57 points, and an average of 16.6 points allowed — in just the first half!
  • McCarthy’s teams in those five games committed 41 penalties for 305 yards. That’s an average of 8.2 penalties per game, and 61 penalty yards per game. McCarthy’s teams had no less than six penalties in any game, and had a high of 14.
  • An 0-5 record.

Now, sure, the past doesn’t always indicate the future. I’m sure there is plenty of context that could be spun in McCarthy’s favor to explain away those results. I’m just noting a pattern. And when you pair those results with two major public blowups about his work ethic during his career, and an ultimately disappointing tenure in Dallas — I think any reasonable person would agree there is at the very least reason to be skeptical that McCarthy will achieve better results in Pittsburgh. I want McCarthy to live up to the quarterback developer line we were sold. Maybe he can. That certainly would be best and most convenient for Pittsburgh.

But is it realistic?

Again, I’m not predicting the Steelers will remove him. But if Art Rooney II is serious about returning this team to greatness, he shouldn’t just handwave this incident and continue business as usual. The rest of this season should be an audition for McCarthy. Any more rumblings of sleeping on the job, skipping meetings, and not doing the weekly prep should be grounds for moving on. A collapse down the stretch, getting blown out in the Wild Card round, or losing the locker room, should be too. IF McCarthy is in any way cutting corners, or just too disorganized to live up to the NFL standard, any serious organization would move on.

All we can do as fans is hope that’s what this team can be again, and soon.

But that’s enough for the day. Celebrate this win. Flush the drama and be glad we’re on to Houston.

Let’s break it down.

1-2-3, Steelers!

Let us know what you think in the comments. Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more!

item.title: Bears Week 12 Flashbacks: Arrowhead Upset, Hester’s Magic, Turkey Day
item.description: Hop aboard the Gridiron Time Machine with @iamcogs and take a trip down Week 12 Bears memory lane!
item.content:encoded:
In this week’s edition of the Gridiron Time Machine, we’re revisiting an unlikely comeback at Arrowhead, a valuable lesson in why you should never kick to Devin Hester, and a Thanksgiving victory that came down to the final second. So hop aboard the time machine for another fantastic trip down memory lane.

1.) 1993, Bears @ Chiefs: An unlikely comeback at Arrowhead

November 21, 1993 | Bears win 19-17

The Bears entered Week 12 of the 1993 season with a 4-5 record under first-year head coach Dave Wannstedt. A trip to Arrowhead Stadium to face the 7-2 Kansas City Chiefs wasn’t exactly the ideal opportunity to get back to .500.

Things certainly didn’t look promising early on, as future Hall of Fame running back Marcus Allen found the end zone twice to give Kansas City a 14-0 lead in the second quarter.

The Bears managed to get on the board before halftime thanks to a pair of Kevin Butler field goals from 32 and 45 yards out, cutting the deficit to eight.

Chicago continued chipping away in the third quarter when Tim Worley broke loose for a 25-yard touchdown run. A blocked extra point kept the Bears from pulling within one, and a Nick Lowery field goal extended Kansas City’s lead to 17-12 heading into the fourth quarter.

If you were expecting Jim Harbaugh to lead some sort of aerial assault to complete the comeback, think again.

Harbaugh completed 13 of his 20 pass attempts for just 98 yards and two interceptions, finishing the afternoon with a passer rating of 37.1. He was considerably more effective with his legs, rushing for 56 yards on eight attempts.

The Bears leaned heavily on their ground game, rushing for 185 yards on 43 attempts. Worley led the way with 59 yards, while Neal Anderson added another 42.

With just over three minutes remaining, Anderson punched it in from one yard out to give Chicago its first lead of the afternoon. The Bears’ defense, which recorded five sacks and held Kansas City to just three second-half points, made sure that lead stuck.

The Chiefs would go on to win the AFC West and reach the AFC Championship Game that season, but on this particular Sunday, the Bears had their number.

Winning on the road against one of the AFC’s best teams without throwing for 100 yards?

That’s some Chicago Bears football right there.

2.) 2007, Bears vs. Broncos: Denver learns not to kick to Hester

November 25, 2007 | Bears win 37-34 (OT)

Coming off their Super Bowl appearance the previous season, the 2007 Chicago Bears found themselves sitting at 4-6 entering Week 12. While the season hadn’t gone according to plan, the Bears still had one of the most electrifying players in football at their disposal.

Apparently, Denver Broncos punter Todd Sauerbrun wasn’t particularly concerned.

Leading up to the game, Sauerbrun made it known that the Broncos weren’t planning on kicking away from Devin Hester.

You can probably guess where this is going.

Trailing 13-6 early in the third quarter, Hester fielded a Sauerbrun punt and returned it 75 yards for a touchdown, tying the game at 13.

Denver eventually regained the lead on a five-yard touchdown run by Cecil Sapp, setting up another opportunity for Hester on the ensuing kickoff.

This time, he took it 88 yards to the house.

Two return touchdowns in the same quarter, covering a combined 163 yards. Perhaps kicking away from Hester wasn’t such a bad idea after all.

Despite Hester’s heroics, the Bears still found themselves trailing 34-20 in the fourth quarter. A young quarterback by the name of Jay Cutler was having himself quite an afternoon, completing 17 of 31 passes for 302 yards, two touchdowns and an interception.

Yes, that Jay Cutler.

Adrian Peterson cut Denver’s lead to seven with a four-yard touchdown run before the Bears’ special teams came through again, blocking a punt and giving Chicago another opportunity to tie the game.

With 28 seconds remaining, Rex Grossman connected with Bernard Berrian for a three-yard touchdown to send the game into overtime. Robbie Gould put the finishing touches on the comeback with a 39-yard field goal, giving Chicago a 37-34 victory.

The Bears won despite committing four turnovers and surrendering 430 yards of total offense.

Of course, it helps when arguably the greatest return specialist in NFL history is spotting your offense 14 points.

Lesson learned, Denver.

3.) 2021, Bears @ Lions: Santos saves Thanksgiving

November 25, 2021 | Bears win 16-14

There wasn’t much for either team to be thankful for heading into this Thanksgiving Day matchup. The Bears were riding a five-game losing streak, while the Detroit Lions were still searching for their first victory under head coach Dan Campbell.

With rookie quarterback Justin Fields sidelined by a rib injury, veteran Andy Dalton got the starting nod for Chicago.

Detroit struck first when Jared Goff connected with Josh Reynolds for a 39-yard touchdown in the opening quarter. The Bears responded with 13 unanswered points in the second quarter, highlighted by a 17-yard touchdown pass from Dalton to Jimmy Graham.

Goff helped Detroit reclaim the lead late in the third quarter, finding T.J. Hockenson for a 17-yard touchdown to put the Lions ahead 14-13.

What followed was a rather impressive display of clock management by the Bears.

Taking possession with 8:30 remaining in the fourth quarter, Chicago methodically worked its way down the field. Dalton connected with Damiere Byrd for a pair of crucial third-down conversions, the second of which came after Detroit was penalized for calling consecutive timeouts.

Byrd’s seven-yard reception gave Chicago a first down at the Detroit four-yard line, allowing the Bears to kneel three times and leave just one second on the clock.

Watch the full game highlights on YouTube by clicking below:

Cairo Santos stepped onto the field and connected on a 28-yard field goal as time expired, capping an 18-play, 69-yard drive that consumed the final 8:30 of regulation.

Lost in the excitement of the game-winning drive was a pretty solid performance from Dalton, who completed 24 of 39 passes for 317 yards, a touchdown and an interception. Darnell Mooney accounted for 123 of those yards on just five receptions, while Santos converted all three of his field goal attempts.

The Bears snapped their five-game losing streak and improved to 4-7, while the Lions fell to 0-10-1.

It wasn’t the prettiest Thanksgiving Day football game you’ll ever see, but the Bears walked away with a victory over a division rival.

And Bears fans could finally enjoy their Thanksgiving dinner without a side of disappointment.

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

item.title: Big Blue View mailbag: Jameis Winston, J.J. McCarthy, playoffs, more
item.description: The mail’s here! Questions, answers as the Giants prepare for Week 12.
item.content:encoded:
Michael Buscemi asks: Really curious about this question and answer at least in every game there is a few times a cornerback or safety drops an interception do they ever have drills for defensive backs from quarterbacks that train their hands better to catch and making deceptions it happened so often I’m just curious to see what your answer is about practicing drills to help control the ball.

Ed says: Michael, these guys are at the highest level of their sport. They practice catching the ball every day — or at least every day there is a practice. There are always drills that involve catching the ball, both standing still and on the move. There is also a JUGS machine guys can use at the end of practice. Several players use it all the time.

Reality is, though, game and practice conditions are much different. You practice the fundamentals of catching so that it becomes muscle memory, but you can’t mimic game speed or circumstances.

John Steinbreder asks: As is the case with so many Giants fans, I am enjoying every part of the Jameis Winston Experience and the deft and very selfless ways he has been performing his duties as QB2 for the Giants. And that has me wondering: has there ever been a back-up quite like him? The thoughtful mentoring of the young signal callers. Coming in off the bench when needed to win games. And now his role as the man orchestrating the tush-push, whether as a runner or passer. Then, of course, there are the signals he actually calls, in part to try and draw the opposing team offsides and also to entertain. And his barking, “Who Let The Dogs Out” in the Commanders game still has me chortling weeks later.  

I am also curious as to your thoughts on Harbaugh utilizing Jameis in those situations as a way of protecting JJ from taking unnecessary shots. It makes me think back to Tom Coughlin who never called QB sneaks with Eli because he did not want to expose him unnecessarily to injury. It’s a pretty smart move on Harbaugh’s part, to protect JJ and also to keep Jameis engaged and involved.

Ed says: John, there have been many veteran backup quarterbacks over the years who have willingly helped younger players learn their craft. There have been backups/journeymen with flamboyant personalities like Ryan Fitzpatrick. Winston, though, is one of a kind.

He willingly embraced helping Jaxson Dart. Even after J.J. McCarthy was given his starting job, Winston has embraced doing everything he can to help McCarthy and the team as a whole.

This guy is a team captain, a member of the team’s leadership council and the guy who breaks down the team’s pre-game on-field huddle. I don’t know of a backup quarterback who has carried that kind of respect from his teammates.

As for the QB sneak stuff, I think there are two parts to it. I think it is something that Winston does well — not all quarterbacks have the feel for it, or really want to throw themselves into that scrum. Also, Harbaugh likes to find some type of role for everyone on the game day roster.

John Harbaugh answered a question about Winston and the QB sneaks on Friday.

“He’s good at it,” Harbaugh said. “I think originally, probably, it was something he had been repping already, and so it was one less thing on J.J.’s (quarterback J.J. McCarthy) plate. Just being honest, I’d probably say that was kind of where we started with it. We kind of got to the point where if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. It’s been good for us. It ends up being a whole package for us.”

Paul Staunton asks: At this point, what percentage of the Giants’ playbook can the OC use when JJ is in the game?

Ed says: Paul, my understanding is that there are no limitations at this point. Now, you also have to understand that there are dozens of plays, if not more than that, in the playbook that will never get used. But, the point is the Giants are not limited by McCarthy’s knowledge at this point.

Thomas Fergus asks: What is going on with Darius Alexander? Many of us had high expectations of him contributing to the defense this year. He flashed strong play and now is invisible and getting healthy scratched. Has he lost the trust of Wilson? We need all hands on deck for the playoffs, will Alexander get on the field at any point left this year?

Ed says: Thomas, the fact that Alexander was not active last Sunday against the Jacksonville Jaguars was curious. C.J. Okoye got a uniform instead of Alexander against the Jacksonville Jaguars, and had a nice game. It could have been as simple as the Giants feeling that Okoye had a really nice week of practice and deserved to play. If that was the case, he rewarded them.

Alexander had been trending up, but his play vs. Washington in Week 10 wasn’t good. Perhaps not getting a uniform was a message. He will play when the coaching staff believes he deserves to play.

James Pauloski asks: Last week Kayvon Thibideaux intercepted a pass on an attempted two point conversion. Why isn’t that recorded as an interception by him?

Ed says: The play is scored as an extra-point try, not an offensive or defensive play. No stats are recorded. Players don’t get credit for pass completetions/catches/rushing yards/tackles, or anything else.

Thibodeaux chose not to run the ball out of the end zone. Had he returned it all the way for a score, it would have been two points for the Giants.

Vincent Moody asks: Hi, one thing I was wondering about. The Giants O- line hasn’t been good at all, especially at run-blocking. The Eagles moved on from Jeff Stoutland recently. Is he retired or is there any chance he would come over to the Giants.

Ed says: Vincent, first I am going to strongly disagree with the notion that the offensive line “hasn’t been good at all.”

  • Pro Football Network ranks the Giants’ line 19th overall, 10th-best in the league blocking for the pass and just 30th for the run.
  • Pro Football Focus ranks the Giants’ line sixth in pass-blocking, 31st in run-blocking. PFF has the Giants 15th overall.
  • NFL Lines ranks the Giants 21st overall.

The Giants are an average to slightly below league average line overall, and one of the better pass-blocking units in the NFL. There is no doubt they need to do a better job clearing holes for running backs.

As for Jeff Stoutland, I have no idea whether or not he plans to return to coaching after this season. I would think he will have his choice of jobs, should he want to coach. I suppose it’s possible, but I don’t sense unhappiness with current offensive line coach Mike Bloomgren.

Joe Castronova asks: Along with most Giant fans, and likely the rest of the NFL, Harbaugh’s leadership has been impressive. It stands out even more given the situation in Pittsburgh. What can you see is the primary difference between what we are getting with Harbaugh versus coaches in the past?

Ed says: Joe, Harbaugh has brought a great many things to the Giants. His experience and previous success brought instant credibility. He brought an established way of doing things. Players understand who is in charge and what the standard is.

There is no facade with Harbaugh. Everybody knows where they stand. Shoot, even I know where I stand with him. In my view, Joe Judge tried to be something he wasn’t — a Bill Belichick tough guy. Brian Daboll forgot that when you are the head coach you can’t be everybody’s buddy, and when things don’t go the way you want alienating your coaches isn’t great.

Players believe what Harbaugh tells them, even if it isn’t always what they want to hear.

Matthew Burns asks: We know Jameis is under contract for 2027. If JJ continues to win and show developmental progress, how high of a draft pick do you think the Giants will be asking for? And do you think there is a team or teams willing to pay that price?

Ed says: Matthew, what willl happen this offseason is guesswork at this point. As of right now, I think the proper course of action is to trade McCarthy for the best haul of draft picks the Giants can get. Coul that change? Sure? Might John Harbaugh have a different opinion than mine? Sure.

I think McCarthy has already done enough to warrant a return that is more valuable than the fifth-round pick the Giants used to get him. I think he has shown he can start in the NFL. How high of a pick they can get, or they will ask for, depends on what happens the next few weeks.

Are there teams that would be willing to pay a good price for McCarthy? Absolutely. There are more quarterback-needy teams than there will be good quarterbacks in the draft. Teams like the Steelers, Browns, Colts, Cardinals and a few others could use quarterbacks and might have won enough games that they won’t be at the top of the market.

Could the Giants get a first-round pick in return? If a team like Pittsburgh is desperate enough, maybe.

Bruce Noble asks: Do you think that Harbaugh will (or should) takeover offensive play calling?

Ed says: No, Bruce. To my knowledge, Harbaugh has never called offensive — or defensive — plays. He is a CEO head coach. Why should a change in play callers be considered, anyway? Because there have been a couple of play calls you didn’t like?

When the Giants mystifyingly chose to throw the ball on 12 of 13 plays while trying to protect the lead Sunday against Jacksonville, do you think that was offensive coordinator Matt Nagy going rogue? Or, do you think maybe he was following instruction to put the game in the quarterback’s hands? All the head coach has to do is lean into the headset and say “run the ball.”

The Giants are in first place. They are 14th in the league in points scored despite being on their third quarterback, being second in the league in fumbles, and having an offensive line that has been awful when it comes to blocking for the run. Why do things need to be changed?

Barry Block asks: Have you heard anything lately about Tracy’s return? More importantly, what is his likely impact, when/if that happens? At least they won’t have to give the ball to Skattebo just because they don’t have anyone else.

Ed says: Barry, Tracy is eligible to return from IR after the game this weekend against the Indianapolis Colts. I would expect him to be activated, and to go back to being a primary kickoff returner and part of a rotation with Cam Skattebo. That is pretty much where things were when he got hurt.

Jeffrey Faulkner asks: This may be hard to answer, but is young Mr. Skattebo wearing on Coach Harbaugh? I know he’s a polarizing individual, but I was curious if there is any sense that you’ve potentially seen or felt that his antics are getting to Harbaugh? Not necessarily the fumbles, that I get from a head coach they should be annoyed. But clips during games after Skattebo being intense in his way seems like Harbs isn’t having it. I know he’s got a lot of spinning plates, and it may not be because of skat or it’s a heat of the moment thing and after the game’s things mellow. Just curious if you’ve got a feeling being around them.

Ed says: Jeffrey, I don’t know that Skattebo is “wearing” on Harbaugh. I don’t think Harbaugh appreciated Skattebo’s backflip at the end of the game against the Jaguars.

I do think Harbaugh has made it clear that he believes the Giants need an upgrade from Skattebo as RB1.

Spencer Gross asks: Giants wanna be a run team. How do we fix this next year? I know the draft is anyone’s guess as there’s always risers and fallers but would it be wise to draft some “hog mollies” this coming year? Kade Piper at center and Evan Tengesdahl at left guard sounds nice. Thoughts?

Ed says: Spencer, I say every year that it is wise to use draft capital on the offensive and defensive lines. That won’t change during the upcoming draft. I think the Giants will hope for improvement from Sisi Mauigoa, and it will be interesting to see what they do at center and left guard. As for specific players, I haven’t spent a single minute studying the 2027 NFL Draft class yet.

Also, see my answer above the running back situation.

Fletcher Wyman asks: Clearly we had a schematic problem with Bowen trying to play Adebo and Banks in zone when they are both natural press man corners and working well in Dennard’s hybrid system. With the Newsome injury it feels like Adebo is playing himself into the final year of his contract being realized. I would love to keep Banks even with his PI reputation but if we can’t get a deal done with him is he worth the 23(?)M tag next year? Tag and trade? Tag with hopes of reaching a deal before the full bill comes due? Transition tag and see how the league feels about him?

Ed says: Fletcher, Deonte Banks has been one of the better cornerbacks in the NFL this season. The Giants are going to do everything the can to keep him.

There were reports that the Giants tried to get a deal done with Banks during the bye week, but were unable to.

Per NextGen Stats, Banks is allowing a career-low 68.7 passer rating against. He have given up just 26 completions on 56 targets, a career-best 46.4%.

One more note from NGS:

Banks has recorded 14 passes defensed this season, tied for the most among outside cornerbacks, with a 25.0% ball hawk rate that is tied with Sauce Gardner and Davison Igbinosun for fourth-highest (minimum 20 targets).

The Giants would, I’m sure, prefer to get a long-term deal done with Banks like they did with Greg Newsome. Would they use the tag on Banks? I have not asked GM Joe Schoen this, but I think they would if it became necessary.

David DeFilippo asks: I’ve kind of lost track, but of the dozen or so players currently on IR are there any who could be activated before the end of the season who still might contribute something meaningful to the playoff push? Also, which of these players do you think are in the plans for next season?

Ed says: David, the IR list is as follows:

WR Calvin Austin, CB Jarrick Bernard-Converse, WR Braxton Berrios, OLB Brian Burns, QB Jaxson Dart, CB Thaddeus Dixon, LB Tremaine Edmunds, DE Chauncey Golston, CB Greg Newsome, WR Gunner Olszewski, DT Roy Robertson-Harris, RB Tyrone Tracy.

Tracy should be back next week. The Giants hope Newsome will play again this year. Other than that, we’re talking about next year — including for Jaxson Dart.

Dart Burns, Austin, Edmunds, Robertson-Harris and maybe a couple of others are probably in the team’s future plans.

Scott Fraser asks: As of right now who wins the division in your opinion as a Giants fan?

Ed says: Scott, I believe that if the Giants win on Sunday they will win the division. I think that if they were to lose on Sunday, not having the tiebreaker vs. the Washington Commanders will haunt them. Anything can happen, of course, but that would be my gut feeling right now.

Brian Scott asks: I saw something recently where JJ McCarthy was talking about working on throwing with more touch. That made me wonder … I know that most quarterbacks have private coaches. Are players allowed to work with private coaches during the season, or is that prohibited by the team (or by the CBA)? And if it’s allowed, how does the team manage the interactions between players, private coaches, and position coaches? Presumably, everyone is working toward a common goal, but it still seems like it could get messy and possibly counterproductive.

Ed says: Brian, McCarthy works with former NFL quarterback John Beck at the 3DQB quarterback training school during the offseason.

These are offseason trainers. They don’t come in to team facilities and work with their clients during the season. That is what teams have offensive coordinators and quarterback coaches for. To my knowledge, working with a private coach during the season isn’t prohibited by the CBA. When, though, would there be time? These guys already put in loooooong days. Also, I would think doing so might be looked at as a slap in the face to a team’s coaching staff.

What players do with private coaches during the offseason is their business. Every coach teaches slightly differently, even if they are striving to teach the same thing. I do know that teams are aware of who their players work with, and team and private coaches often have relationships. Neither side wants their work to be counter-productive, but teams can’t control how private coaches instruct clients.

Howard Stern asks: The NY Giants front office is a bit of an NFL outlier – a titled general manager, a head coach with personnel input and a SVP of operations and strategy with significant experience at the team and league levels. Many BBV’ers take wild guesses at who is doing what, especially when it comes to trades and signings. Do you have any insight you can share regarding how our front office responsibilities are delegated and shared?

Ed says: Howard, is the Giants’ front office really an outlier? I would say more and more front offices are structured with the head coach being the top guy on the decision-making chart right now. Sean McVay, Sean Payton, Andy Reid, Jim Harbaugh, and probably a bunch of other teams are led by strong head coaches.

The only thing that might be unusual is that Dawn Aponte reports to Harbaugh, not to GM Joe Schoen. Still, Aponte and Schoen have known each other for a long while.

I can’t give you the inner workings because I’m not in those discussions.

Dale Albeck asks: I have been wondering how a routine week between Sunday games breakdown? It appears they don’t do any on field practice until Wednesday.  So Monday and Tuesday is rest and what else? Film work?  Also, when do they come into the facility and how long are they there?  When do position groups get together and for how long? This would really shine a light on how long a week of work is for the guys. 

Ed says: Dale, every team is somewhat different. And, there are so many non-Sunday games now that staying in a routine can be difficult. But, a Sunday-to-Sunday week looks something like this.

Monday — Film review, on-field corrections in a walk-through, injury treatments, and a weightlifting session.

Tuesday — Players day off. Many will be around the facility for at least part of the day, anyway, getting treatment, watching film, lifting weights. Recovery is critical, and there is no better place to do it than at the team facility.

Wednesday — The first practice of the week. Game plans are generally installed in a lighter, unpadded practice. There are lots of meetings, which vary in length from team to team.

Thursday — If there is going to be a padded practice, this would be the one. There are always meetings galore, and lifting.

Friday — This might be a relatively shorter day for players. Thursday and Friday practice feature a lot of situational work.

Saturday — A final meeting and walk-through, and generally travel for the road team.

Wayne Wright asks: Is it my imagination, or do the Giants almost never run slant routes with Malik Nabers? The slant was OBJ’s bread and butter back in the day and I see a lot of other teams run slants with their No. 1 receiver. Doesn’t it seem like this is a play the Giants should run with Nabers more often than what we see?

Ed says: Wayne, no two players are the same. Just because a play was great for Odell Beckham doesn’t mean it will be a great play for Malik Nabers.

I can’t find anything not behind a paywall to tell me what the exact numbers are, but it is clear from the charts at NextGen Stats that both the Daboll-Kafka and Harbaugh-Nagy staffs preferred to get the ball to Nabers on the outside.

Chris Barbosa asks: With the tie that we had with the Commanders and the confusion I see some fans have with the half a game why doesn’t the NFL just get rid of the tie? College football no longer play to a tie and has a system. Look at hockey, they no longer have ties. The only league that has a tie is the NFL. To me sports should never end in a tie. I think I have an idea to stop ties from happening in the NFL.Start off the overtime period with no time. Have both teams have possession of the ball. If they both score a touchdown or both score a field goal then you go to sudden death 10 minute quarter. What do you think?

Ed says: Chris, nobody likes a tie game. For the NFL, though, the overtime rule is a compromise that involves player safety. They don’t want regular-season games going on endlessly. Thus, the 10-minute limit. It’s not perfect, but I can live with it.

Submit a question

Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.
