item.title: Final Audition: 3 fixes Michael Penix needs to save his Falcons future
item.description: Seven games remain for Michael Penix Jr. to fix three glaring flaws—and prove he deserves to remain Atlanta’s starter.
item.content:encoded:
Atlanta Falcons quarterback Michael Penix exits the Week 11 bye and enters a seven-game stretch that could define his career. With scrutiny mounting, the final two months of 2026 will not only dictate whether Penix remains the Falcons’ starter entering 2027, but could also determine whether he ever gets another shot to lead an NFL franchise.

To save his job, Penix must show immediate growth in three critical areas: starting faster, surviving pocket pressure, and rediscovering his signature deep ball.

Penix must fix his first-quarter freeze

According to Next Gen Stats, the Falcons’ slow starts have been fueled by a 31st-ranked first-quarter EPA per play and 32nd-ranked first-quarter passing yards. Leaning on the run game would help, with Atlanta’s early-game run rate plummeting from 56 percent in Penix’s first three starts to the 24th-ranked 42 percent over the last five. But the Falcons cannot ask star running back Bijan Robinson to carry the entire offense, as Penix has to pull some weight.

Per NFL.com, Penix has completed 46 percent of his throws in the first quarter while averaging just 3 yards per attempt. The Falcons have produced just six passing first downs in the first quarter in Penix’s eight starts, compared with an NFL average of 19. This keeps the team from sustaining offense, thanks to a league-low first-quarter third-down efficiency of 10 percent across Penix’s starts. This isn’t a problem unique to 2026, as Penix posted a dismal 38.8 passer rating in the first quarter during his rookie season before surging to 108.8 in his second.

That leap offers hope that more time in Tommy Rees’ offense can spark a similar turnaround. But as a third-year pro, Penix’s early-game struggles are harder to excuse, and Atlanta cannot afford to wait until 2027 for competence.

Pressure is Penix’s kryptonite

While the slow starts are problematic, they at least show growth potential. However, Penix’s biggest issue is his inability to handle pressure. Rarely do quarterbacks thrive under pressure, but few struggle as much as Penix.

Per Next Gen Stats, Penix’s completion percentage over expected (CPOE) plummets by a league-worst 13 percentage points when pressured. Remarkably, the chasm between Penix and the NFL’s second-worst passer under pressure (Jameis Winston) is just as wide as the gap between Winston and the next eight quarterbacks on the list. Penix’s struggles against pressure are in a tier of their own.

PFF’s marks on Penix under pressure are even more stark. He has the league’s lowest passing grade, and his turnover-worthy-play rate of 11.8 percent is the worst in the league when under pressure. Unlike Penix’s poor early-game numbers, there aren’t many signs of optimism, as his PFF metrics have steadily declined since entering the NFL. It’s hard not to conclude that his 2025 injury has made Penix more tentative. But it’s been a known issue since college: if you can move him off his spot, his efficiency falls off a cliff.

As the Falcons look to rebuild their offensive line this offseason, patience won’t be on Penix’s side. Even with former offensive lineman Ian Cunningham as general manager and legendary line coach Bill Callahan in the building, rebuilding Atlanta’s trenches won’t be an overnight fix. Just ask Matt Ryan, now the man who’ll weigh in on Penix’s future, after he endured relentless pressure during his final seasons when the Falcons launched their last major offensive line overhaul in 2019. Young linemen take time to gel, meaning Atlanta needs a quarterback who can survive behind a transitional front, not one who crumbles the moment he feels some heat. Penix doesn’t appear to be that option unless he shows improvement over what remains of 2026.

Where did Penix’s deep ball go?

Penix’s flaws would be easier to live with if his greatest strength offset them. Penix’s best asset has always been his bazooka of a left arm, which should translate into his ability to hit downfield shots. While PFF ranks him 15th overall with a 48 percent adjusted completion rate on deep passes over 20 yards, that number is heavily skewed by his first three starts when he was nearly flawless save for a Jahan Dotson drop against Green Bay. Over his last five games, Penix’s deep-ball accuracy has cratered to 29 percent (29th in the NFL).

Penix desperately needs to get back to capitalizing on his greatest strength if he’s going to be Atlanta’s starter moving forward. Atlanta’s loss to Kansas City provides a bit of optimism, as Penix hit three deep completions in that game, the most in any game so far this year. However, all three only came after the team fell into a 14-3 hole, again illustrating his tendency to start slowly.

The bar is low, but the clock is ticking

Young quarterbacks experiencing ups and downs is the norm in the NFL, but it’s easier to accept the lows when they’re also delivering highs. Especially for a team like the Falcons that is struggling to win games. Wins and losses get pinned on quarterbacks, fairly or not. What Penix can control is showing the arm talent that made him a top-10 pick. Without it, there isn’t much to love about Penix’s play lately.

Improvement over the next seven games in these three key areas will justify the Falcons continuing their investment in Penix. Any progress Penix shows for the rest of 2026 can create momentum heading into the offseason. Without it, Penix’s future as a starter is in jeopardy. The Falcons will have to decide whether to pick up Penix’s fifth-year option this offseason. If they don’t exercise that option, 2027 will mark the final year of his rookie contract and his last real shot at a starting role. And it may not even be a guaranteed shot if the team pivots this offseason.

Outside of vertical passing, the bar Penix needs to clear isn’t that high. He must be dynamic downfield to justify his draft pedigree, yet he only needs to climb to league-average efficiency in the first quarter. Given his history, pressure may always be his fatal flaw, but he just needs to improve from awful to run-of-the-mill bad. Glimpses of progress are there, including his willingness to scramble in Madrid as he gains more confidence on his surgically repaired knee.

The path for Penix’s progress is laid out. All he needs to do is walk it.

item.title: Detroit Lions’ playoff, NFC North odds still high despite loss to Bears
item.description: The Detroit Lions’ playoff, NFC North, No. 1 seed, and Super Bowl odds still remain high despite loss to Bears.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions’ loss to the Chicago Bears was deflating and disappointing. Not so much because it was a critical game for Detroit’s playoff odds, but because the Lions were in a prime position to win and take a stranglehold on the division.

But as you’ll soon see, the Lions are still in a great position to accomplish everything in front of them. Let’s look at how their playoff, NFC North, and even Super Bowl odds have shifted after their Thanksgiving loss to the Bears.

Postseason odds:

NYT simulator:78% (down 8%)
RBSDM:81% (down 4%)
DVOA: 83.3% (down 6.3%)
ESPN (FPI):91.5% (down 5.5%)

Even by the most pessimistic models, the Lions still have more than a 3-in-4 chance to make the postseason. Their loss to the Bears did not decrease their postseason odds by more than 10% across any of these four prediction models. ESPN still remains very high on the Lions, with a massive 91.5% chance to make the playoffs, but it seems like the more normal average is around 80-83%.

NFC North title odds

NYT simulator:15% (down 14%)
RBSDM:20% (down 13%)
DVOA:19.3% (down 18%)
ESPN (FPI):30.6% (down 19.4%)

Obviously, this loss had a bigger impact on Detroit’s chances to win the division, but the odds are not outstandingly long still. The Lions still have a 15-30% chance to win the NFC North, and that stands true because they still have three division games left. And while they’re all on the road, Detroit has proven they can go toe-to-toe with any of those teams. And the fact that Detroit has a 2-1 record in the division already gives them a nice leg up on the tiebreakers, as long as they continue to beat their divisional foes.

NFC’s No. 1 seed

NYT simulator: 4% (down 4%)
RBSDM:6% (down 6%)
DVOA:3.9% (down 6.3%)
ESPN: 5% (down 6%)

You can pretty much kiss the Lions’ odds for the No. 1 seed goodbye. Unless the San Francisco 49ers struggle down the stretch—and they do have tough games against the Seahawks, Giants, Rams, and Chiefs left—Detroit is not likely to finish any higher than the NFC’s No. 2 seed.

Super Bowl appearance odds

ESPN (FPI):11.0% (down 1.9%)
DVOA:7.3% (down 3.1%)

Surprisingly, the Lions’ Super Bowl odds have not been impacted too much. Perhaps their strong offensive performance against a decent Bears defense has fed the models’ optimism about Detroit being able to survive a shootout game. However, their defensive performance on Thursday looms large as well.

item.title: Bo Nix: I saw Jalen Ramsey, just didn't throw it high enough over his head on interception
item.description: Broncos quarterback Bo Nix threw a truly baffling pick-six to Steelers cornerback Jalen Ramsey in Friday's loss, and afterward he said it was just a bad throw, not a bad read.
item.content:encoded:
Broncos quarterback Bo Nix threw a truly baffling pick-six to Steelers cornerback Jalen Ramsey in Friday's loss, and afterward he said it was just a bad throw, not a bad read.

Nix threw the ball directly to Ramsey, who was not particularly close to any Broncos receiver, which led to questions about what Nix was looking at. Nix said he thought he could throw the ball deep over Ramsey's head and threw it way too short.

"I saw him, just didn't throw it high enough over his head," Nix said.

The Steelers' first touchdown was also Nix's fault, as he dropped the football into the end zone, where T.J. Watt jumped on it.

"Going down 7-0 with a fumble recovered in the end zone for a touchdown is not ideal," Nix said. "That started us off on the wrong foot and we couldn't get out of the hole after that."

It was a miserable game from Nix, but he said the Broncos will move on to the next game. One in which they hope their quarterback won't hand the other team two touchdowns.

item.title: Cowboys news: Jerry Jones will ‘question everything’ after Eagles loss

item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys blew a three touchdown lead to the Philadelphia Eagles on Thanksgiving, and Jerry Jones says that there won’t be anything that he won’t review as a result. Brian Schottenheimer and his philosophy is not getting it done, and it may ultimately cost him his job.

New defensive play-caller Mike Pettine produced mixed results through two games as Dallas looks for answers on that side of the ball.

Jerry to ‘question everything’ after Cowboys’ ‘damning’ Thanksgiving loss – Jeremy Bergman, NFL.com

The Cowboys blew a 21-point lead to the Eagles. As a result, team owner Jerry Jones is contemplating a bunch of issues in Dallas.

The Cowboys owner said he did not anticipate making any coaching changes ahead of Dallas’ next game, a Week 13 matchup with the Seattle Seahawks 11 days away, but that didn’t mean Schottenheimer was free from criticism.

“These are setbacks and they’re damning setbacks, there’s no question about it,” Jones said, via ESPN. “And especially when we feel like that we can look at parts of the game where it was ours to take and we didn’t. So when you look at every bit of it, then you have to question everything.”

Dak Prescott has a telling response to coaching change question after Cowboys’ devastating loss to the Eagles – Mauricio Rodriguez, AtoZ Sports

The job security of Brian Schottenheimer is certainly in question at the moment. However, Dak Prescott pretty much avoided the topic when he was asked about it.

Toward the end of the press conference, Prescott was asked how he would feel if there were a coaching change over the next 11 days. He did not take the opportunity to endorse Schottenheimer or his coaching staff, which is something you’d expect him to do in a different context. Maybe he didn’t take the question that way.

Instead, he said: “I don’t know what you are alluding to, so I’m going to focus on doing what I can, the best I can, controlling what I can, and handling whatever comes when it comes, as I just tried to do in life.”

Brian Schottenheimer, Cowboys ‘ready to get back to work’ after Thanksgiving loss to Eagles – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com

After Dallas lost its fourth game while scoring over 30 points, head coach Brian Schottenheimer prepares to roll up his sleeves for the last five games.

On a conference call Friday, Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said he spoke to both Jerry Jones and COO/co-owner Stephen Jones Thursday night following the loss.

“They share in our disappointment,” Schottenheimer said of his conversations with the Jones family. “Again, we felt like we had an opportunity to win that game. An important game, divisional game against a division rival. Our conversations were shared disappointment, but also, we’re ready to get back to work.”

Small sample size yields mixed results for Cowboys’ switch at defensive play-caller – Calvin Watkins, Dallas Morning News

Mike Pettine has called the defensive plays in place of Christian Parker for two games now. There’s been some positives, but some of the same glaring issues continue to show up.

In two games with new defensive play-caller Mike Pettine, the Cowboys have allowed 69 points and 715 yards.

They’ve also allowed four plays of 25 or more yards, with three of those going for touchdowns.

“Again, small size,” coach Brian Schottenheimer said of the switch from Christian Parker to Pettine. “I thought the sacks have been really a positive thing. Where we got in trouble [Thursday] was the quarterback got out. We weren’t able to keep Joe [Milton] contained very well and, quite honestly, we had guys in position and in one-on-one ops down the field, their guys made the plays and we didn’t.”

Brian Schottenheimer’s culture has failed on the field. It will cost him his job – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram

The Cowboys have continued to be inconsistent no matter what Brian Schottenheimer has come up with. It could lead to his demise in Dallas.

When leads are in-hand on your home turf against backup quarterbacks, that elite culture is supposed to show up to make sure that those leads don’t evaporate — but it just isn’t doing so.

Tyler Smith was almost in tears with how angry he was at himself for allowing a fourth-down sack in the final minute that gave Philadelphia a short field and an easier chance at the game-winning field goal. Schottenheimer continued to say that “it starts with us as a coaching staff” once again, because he knows that’s true. Dak Prescott, despite yet another heroic performance, acknowledged what he could have done better.

item.title: Steelers stock report after 27-5 win over Broncos
item.description: Pittsburgh Steelers stock report after their dominant Black Friday win.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers made a statement on Black Friday by dominating the Denver Broncos in Pittsburgh. After one of the most tumultuous and dramatic weeks in franchise history, the team scored two defensive touchdowns to beat a Denver team that had won six straight entering this contest.

As always, here is my weekly stock report after the Steelers’ seventh win of the 2026 campaign.

Stock Up

Secondary

What a performance from what is widely considered to be the weakest group on an otherwise great Steelers defense. Jalen Ramsey made one of the biggest plays of the day near the end of the first half, as he took an interception back 36 yards to the house. It was the first pick-six of Broncos quarterback Bo Nix’s career, and Ramsey’s first since his rookie season. Late in the game, it was rookie Daylen Everette who closed things out with an interception of his own. Everette was making his second consecutive start at corner. Nix posted a 44.7 passer rating as he passed for just 169 yards on 40 passing attempts.

Chunk Plays

I wonder if this is the kind of “spark” Mike McCarthy was looking for when he made the switch to Mason Rudolph early in the week. Rudolph found rookie wideout Germie Bernard open across the middle, as the rookie took it down the field for a long gain of 58 yards. Just plays later, Rudolph found DK Metcalf on a beautiful fade route in the end zone over standout Broncos cornerback Patrick Surtain. Late in the second half, Rudolph placed a ball perfectly down the field into the waiting arms of Roman Wilson for a gain of 37. It was not the prettiest day passing the ball overall for either side, but the explosive plays the Steelers offense found were refreshing to see.

DC Patrick Graham

You can have your opinions about how this Steelers team views their head coach, but the Steelers defense clearly has a ton of respect for Patrick Graham. After everything that happened this week, the defense rallied around their defensive coordinator to put together their best game of the season. Forcing two turnovers, allowing just 2.8 yards per rush, and holding the Broncos to just three points on offense is certainly a way to make a statement.

Stock Down

RB Jaylen Warren

Warren was the breakout star of the Steelers season up until their bye week. However, he has largely struggled since then. The running back posted 15 and 28 yards, respectively, in the team’s first two games out of the bye. Today, Warren carried the ball 20 times for just 46 yards. The otherworldly efficiency that made Warren such a threat in the first half of the season has not been there. Granted, the Steelers offensive line has struggled and been injured over the last few games. Warren will continue to see plenty of work and have some good games, but they may not be as consistent with a less than 100% healthy offensive line.

Tight Ends

Where in the world were the Steelers tight ends today? I know the conditions were less than ideal with rain and wind throughout the game, which makes you think they would have relied on some of their big guys in the passing game more. Pat Freiermuth recorded just one catch for one yard while Darnell Washington left the stadium with no stats today.

Aaron Rodgers

item.title: Should the Cardinals extend any of these defensive backs?
item.description: This time of year, contract extensions are offered
item.content:encoded:
With December fast approaching, this is the time of year that NFL GMs decide to extend player’s contracts that the coaching staff wishes to keep next year and usually beyond.

The Arizona Cardinals recently extended TE Elijah Higgins already this week. There are four defensive backs on the roster whose contracts are up after this season. Should GM Monti Ossenfort reach out and offer extensions?

RELATED: OSSENFORT’S DRAFT PICKS HAVE STRUGGLED

The reason that the month of December is the time of year for contract extensions is two-fold. For one, the coaches have had all season with these players, and they determine which ones they want to retain for next season or which athletes they have no issue with finding gainful employment elsewhere. Secondly, the money paid to these players is debated and weighed against their production versus worth to the roster.

Normally, an extension is a pay raise. Players that are deemed marginal with an impending expired deal usually are not re-signed after the season is over initially. After the free agency has come and gone and the player remains unsigned, the GM may reach out and offer a low-ball contract that would keep the athlete in-house or at the very least, available to compete in training camp. Often, this phone call is the only one his agent received.  

The Cardinals have four young defensive backs whose contracts are up this year. Let’s dive into each one’s production, salary, and value to the team. Which ones, if any, should Ossenfort re-sign? Out of these four listed on the depth chart, King is starting at left corner and Clark is listed as starting nickel. In no particular order….well, okay, let’s just do alphabetical.

CB Kei’Trel Clark

5’-10”, 181 pounds

Age: 25

NFL Draft: 2023 6th round (Cardinals)

40 time: 4.42

PFF grade: 50.5

Contract: 4-years, $4.05 million

Being a smallish body style, Clark has to rely on quickness and has the speed to take the receiver long. Good stop-and-go athleticism and footwork. His zone coverage is full of awareness, but he has below-average functional strength. This hurts him in contested catches. Bigger receivers will nudge and bully him away from the ball which means at times he will give up the big play.

Good instincts, has competitive toughness, and very good reaction skills. Good recovery skills once he is beat and is just an average tackler. He is playing in his fourth season.

2026 stats: 11 games played, 4 starts, 27 total tackles, 1 tackle for loss, 0 sacks, 0 QB hits, 0 pressures, 0 forced fumbles, 0 interceptions, 3 batted passes, 2 missed tackles, 30 defensive targets with 16 completions, and 53.3% pass completions in his area. Defensive snaps: 370 (51%), Special teams snaps: 108 (36%).

CB Kalen King

5’-11”, 190 pounds

Age: 23

NFL Draft: 2024 7th round (Packers)

40 time: 4.52

PFF grade: 67.9

Contract: 1-year, $1.05 million

King has played quite a bit this season with the injury to Will Johnson. He doesn’t have that elite speed you want in a cornerback, but he does have quick feet and was considered a ball hawk while at Penn State. He is a willing tackler and a willingness to go beyond his physical traits. King is a very good ball tracker and demonstrates a good blend of agility and speed.

His long speed isn’t good, and has a tendency to lag behind a receiver on deep balls. He is also reliant on two-hand jams in press coverage making him grabby.

2026 stats: 11 games played, 1 start, 20 total tackles, 1 tackle for loss, 0 sacks, 1 QB hit, 0 pressures, 0 forced fumbles, 0 interceptions, 2 batted passes, 2 missed tackles, 21 defensive targets with 16 completions, and 76.2% pass completions in his area. Defensive snaps: 187 (26%), Special teams snaps: 93 (31%).

CB Starling Thomas V

5’-10”, 194 pounds

Age: 26

NFL Draft: 2023 undrafted

40 time: 4.38

PFF grade: not enough snaps to grade

Contract: 1-year, $1.08 million

Speed has never been an issue for Thomas. He has above-average ball skills and has a knack for forcing turnovers. Is a good press corner, but has limitations in man. Great on route recognition and has click-and-close ability.

The knock on him is he is not a shutdown corner, but does offer scheme versatility. He is a bit grabby and his feet aren’t ideal. He will get sloppy in his backpedal and can be sluggish when he is transitioning to close on the ball.

2026 stats: 2 games played, 0 starts, 0 total tackles, 0 tackles for loss, 0 sacks, 0 QB hits, 0 pressures, 0 forced fumbles, 0 interceptions, 0 batted passes, 3 missed tackles. Defensive snaps: 0 (0%), Special teams snaps: 7 (11%).

CB Garrett Williams

5’-10”, 192 pounds

Age: 25

NFL Draft: 2023 3rd round (Cardinals)

40 time: 4.5

PFF grade: 54.2

Contract: 4-years, $5.63 million

One of the Cardinals more experienced cornerbacks, Williams was a three-time All-ACC selection three years while at Syracuse. He has shown excellent ball skills and has decent long ball speed. He reads and reacts instinctively with natural quickness.

He does exhibit undisciplined footwork and has a bad habit of flipping his hips too late in the play which can make him play catchup. But he does recover quickly and is a confident cover corner.

2026 stats: 9 games played, 1 start, 13 total tackles, 0 tackles for loss, 0 sacks, 0 QB hits, 0 pressures, 0 forced fumbles, 0 interceptions, 1 batted pass, 3 missed tackles, 15 defensive targets with 9 completions, and 60.0% pass completions in his area. Defensive snaps: 177 (30%), Special teams snaps: 22 (9%).

item.title: Former St. John Bosco star DJ Uiagalelei excited to be back in the L.A. spotlight
item.description: DJ Uiagalelei, a Southern California high school football star six years ago, will start in place of Justin Herbert when the Chargers face the Patriots.
item.content:encoded:
Stringing together a competent offense has already been challenging enough for the Chargers, who have averaged the NFL’s second-fewest points (16.8) and seventh-fewest yards (288.1) amid a 1-9 start.

Now, they’ll face the New England Patriots on Sunday at SoFi Stadium without Justin Herbert after the quarterback was ruled out for the game after sustaining a concussion against the New York Jets that kept him out of practice all week.

The Chargers will turn to backup quarterback DJ Uiagalelei, who once starred at St. John Bosco High in Bellflower, as they look to capture their second win.

Read more:Justin Herbert remains in concussion protocol, will not play against Patriots

“I’m excited for him,” Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh said. “He’s prepared all season long like every week was going to be the opportunity. Any position, especially quarterback, you want to be prepared. You’d rather be prepared and not have your opportunity than have your opportunity come and not be prepared.”

It’ll be a battle of the backup quarterbacks — Tommy DeVito is starting for the Patriots with Drake Maye out because of a right ankle injury.

Uiagalelei, an undrafted free agent in 2025, has stepped in for Herbert before, but Sunday will mark his first NFL start.

On Nov. 8, during the Chargers’ loss to the Houston Texans, Uiagalelei made his regular-season debut in the fourth quarter and threw a touchdown pass while Herbert was sidelined with a finger injury.

“That was crazy, I ain’t going to lie,” Uiagalelei said.

Sunday, though, will likely be even crazier for the 25-year-old.

“It’s been an unbelievable experience. Unbelievable opportunity, obviously, to get reps with the ones at practice,” Uiagalelei said. “It’s a great opportunity, and I appreciate it.”

Much will be on Uiagalelei’s shoulders as he adapts against New England. In addition, Uiagalelei grew up in Southern California and was even drafted by the Dodgers, so making his NFL starting debut at SoFi Stadium seems appropriate.

Uiagalelei will have plenty of support in the stands, with several loved ones planning to attend the game. He also should have backing from the Chargers’ improved ground game.

Chargers running back Omarion Hampton has run for 194 yards in 36 carries over his last two games and has emerged as a new focal point in offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel’s scheme. Although it did come against teams with losing records, the Chargers have averaged 152 rushing yards in each of the last three games.

Repeating that success likely will be important with the inexperienced Uiagalelei under center.

“I think our blockers are blocking more consistently in a uniform fashion,” McDaniel said of his unit’s encouraging run game. “They’re more tied together consistently. I think the young [linemen], particularly for the rookies … have developed in their run blocking.

“I think a huge impact in the run game the last two weeks has been [Hampton]. I play him about 30 snaps a game, but when he goes into the first quarter and gets two, three, four yards after contact — where other backs wouldn’t — it gets very easy to keep feeding him the ball. It becomes one of my main focuses in the game.”

Read more:NFL Week 12 picks: 49ers defeat Seahawks; Chargers edge out Patriots

The Patriots have a solid run defense, allowing the league’s 12th-fewest rushing yards (106.1) thus far. The Chargers will likely have to overcome that if they want to help their young quarterback succeed.

A stronger defensive effort would help too. Against the Jets, the defense struggled to get the Geno Smith-led offense off the field, and New York scored points on each of its five possessions.

As for Uiagalelei, he says he isn’t nervous about his first NFL start.

“Nerves? They’re good, yeah,” Uiagalelei said with a smile. “I’m excited. You can definitely say that.”

item.title: 3-Point Stance: It’s time for Mike Vrabel’s culture to deliver
item.description: New England’s 2025 fundamentals have faltered
item.content:encoded:
Effort and finish, ball security and disruption, attention to detail, technique and fundamentals, and making great decisions.

Those are the “non-negotiable” pillars Mike Vrabel asked his players to establish entering his first season as the New England Patriots’ head coach in 2025.

Above all, throughout his coaching tenure in Foxboro, Vrabel has repeatedly mentioned the first pillar.

“We are going to demand effort and finish,” Vrabel said in his introductory press conference that offseason. “Our effort and our finish is going to be the contract we make with our teammates.”

The players answered, establishing that culture and helping turn a previously 4-13 win team into the Super Bowl runner-ups in just one offseason.

But 2026’s reality is that the Patriots have largely strayed away from those foundations and from being the highly disciplined group they put on display last season.

And with Drake Maye potentially sidelined for the remainder of the regular season, those standards will have to produce results again as New England looks to Tommy DeVito to keep its 5-5 team’s playoff hopes alive.

Regardless of whether DeVito gives the Patriots opportunities to win, if the players around him continue to make the mistakes that have contributed to the team’s recent struggles, New England will be turning its attention to offseason adjustments come the beginning of January rather than formulating a game plan.

The Patriots must reestablish the fundamentals

Despite Vrabel repeating the importance of effort and finishing at his press conferences, that significance isn’t translating to the field.

Missed tackles and poor execution have told the self-inflicted story of New England’s three most recent losses to the Chicago Bears, Green Bay Packers and Detroit Lions; it’s a recipe that calls for dumping the fresh ingredients in the cooking pot all over the kitchen floor.

Not exactly the instructions you’d want to follow to create that outstanding dish, or any edible plate, for that matter.

Against Chicago, poor tackling efforts allowed 163 yards after the catch, while missed assignments in the secondary against Green Bay allowed Matthew Golden and Christian Watson to combine for 335 receiving yards.

That continued during the team’s trip to Munich, Germany, surrendering nearly 500 yards of offense to Detroit. Hesitant tackling in the open field repeatedly allowed the Lions’ skill players an additional 10-20 yards.

On offense, 35 penalties this season thus far have cut drives short and minimized scoring opportunities. The team’s average of 7.25 total penalties per contest since the Bears matchup ranks them the seventh-most penalized team in the NFL over that time span.

If the Patriots couldn’t consistently win with Maye for those reasons, how will the outcome of their games be any different if their backup signal caller is at the helm?

Tommy DeVito needs help from everyone around him

After taking over for Maye in Munich, DeVito’s offense netted just 94 total yards on 11 drives.

Part of the reason for that lackluster production stems from DeVito stepping into an offensive structure that prioritizes downfield passing to better suit Maye’s abilities. With offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels’ eventual adjustments better matching DeVito’s style of play, his performance is slated to improve.

Still, in addition to the potential chunk plays New England has spent 10 games building the offense around, it’s missing Maye’s out-of-structure playmaking, which allowed him to produce despite being one of the most pressured quarterbacks in the league.

Facing those same circumstances, the odds are stacked against DeVito, who doesn’t possess that same ability.

The most important thing for him to focus on?

Running a smooth operation.

“Managing the offense, being able to get us in and out of the huddle, getting into the right plays and just getting into a flow and a tempo,” Vrabel said on Monday of what the unit needs from the backup.

That entails DeVito properly executing his assignments and prioritizing ball security so the Patriots aren’t playing from behind.

To reflect Vrabel’s desired team identity, the rest of the offense also needs to eliminate the self-inflicted wounds and make great decisions. Meanwhile, the defense must regain its physicality and find ways to create turnovers.

Generating takeaways is a necessity the unit and coaches have been preaching since the summer. Yet, that ideology has yet to come to fruition consistently in the regular season.

That’s a lot of improvements to ask for over the bye week, but that’s the reality New England has been dealt after continuous mishaps in 2026.

Vrabel’s culture faces its biggest test yet

The bye week gives the Patriots an opportunity to correct their mistakes and prepare for life without Maye, who is out for at least six weeks, according to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport. Still, he could be sidelined longer, with Week 17 remaining his earliest possible return.

If New England can’t recoup against a 1-9 Los Angeles Chargers team without Justin Herbert on Sunday, its season outlook would be all but over.

With upcoming matchups against the Buffalo Bills, Kansas City Chiefs, Denver Broncos and Minnesota Vikings, its remaining schedule doesn’t get any easier.

“Believe it or not, [there’s] a lot of positivity,” Dre’Mont Jones said on Tuesday. “We have a lot of confidence that we can turn this thing around. We have a lot of belief in this defense. We believe in Tommy.”

The Patriots have a handful of weeks to prove Vrabel’s culture can once again deliver. Otherwise, they’ll have an entire offseason to figure out why it didn’t click.

“The identity is only as good as the 11 guys prove it to be on the field,” Vrabel said on Tuesday. “So, when we’ve won, [the identity has] been good enough, and when we’ve lost, it hasn’t been good enough. So, that’s been inconsistent … And then ultimately, we’re going to have to exhaust ourselves physically in the way that we need to play.”

Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as Big Blue travels to Indianapolis to battle the Colts tomorrow.

Abdul Carter demanding more from himself after breakout may be key to Giants ‘super challenging’ Colts task | New York Post

Carter, who did not practice Wednesday with the Giants because of a supposedly minor calf/ankle injury, raised the bar of possibilities Sunday with a breakout game (12 quarterback pressures, five quarterback hits and two sacks) followed by his self-description as “the best in the world.”  So, what does the freshly named NFC Defensive Player of the Week have in store Sunday against the Colts and new starting quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr.? 

“Something I said to the team during training camp: What this sport is all about each week is having to prove and re-prove, so gotta do it again,” Carter said. “I could’ve done a lot better — get a couple more sacks — but we’ll see….I think I can be the greatest, so I’m going to keep chasing that.” 

Baldy Breakdown of the Giants offense

NFL Week 12 preview: Picks, predictions | ESPN.com

What we’re hearing on the Giants: The Giants are in an unfamiliar spot as the heavy favorite coming off a huge win at home over the Jaguars. They’re trying to avoid a letdown with the Cowboys and Commanders on their heels in the NFC East. “You don’t treat the Colts any differently than you treat the Jags,” OT Jermaine Eluemunor said. It will be a test to see if these Giants can handle prosperity. 

Stat to know: Giants WR Malik Nabers has grabbed five-plus receptions in eight straight games, which is the fourth-longest active streak in the NFL (Puka Nacua, 17; Jaxon Smith-Njigba, 15; Trey McBride, 13).

Giants finding more defensive line answers as run defense shows progress | USAToday.com

“I think we’re just putting it together. Sometimes it’s a lot of things that kind of come together. People do a good job of creating problems with your gap control. People have a run defense that say, well, we’ve got to stay in our gaps. What does that mean? Well, offenses are doing everything they can to get you out of your gaps,” Harbaugh told reporters this week. “That’s the whole point. That’s the competition of it.

“I think we’ve done a really good job with some of the motions and shifts and different schemes of playing really good, disciplined run defense, and then you’ve got to give the guys credit. The D-line, the tackles, those two veteran tackles are playing great. The depth guys are playing great. Setting edges, the linebackers are playing well, and the DBs are showing up when they’re supposed to.

NFL Week 12 bold predictions: Giants’ Abdul Carter, Cam Skattebo go OFF | NFL.com

Giants’ Carter doubles season sack total for the second time in as many weeks, logging FOUR in Indy. This Sunday at Indianapolis, Carter does just that, doubling last week’s total with four sacks, which inherently doubles his season count to eight. While Carter is dealing with a calf/ankle issue this week, Giants coach John Harbaugh said on Wednesday that “he should be fine for the game.” That’s bad news for the home team. Not only is Anthony Richardson making his first start for the Colts since December of 2024, but Indianapolis’ depleted offensive line is yielding the third-highest pressure rate in the league at 42.6%.

Skattebo dominates Colts on the ground — and stays grounded! There was a ton of buzz around the trade deadline regarding the Giants’ interest in acquiring a running back, such as the Colts’ Jonathan Taylor. Cam Skattebo remains their RB1, however, and he’s the ball-carrier who will score three touchdowns in Indianapolis on Sunday. Now for an even bolder prediction: Skattebo manages to avoid punctuating any of his three scores with a backflip, a sign of growth after his retirement of the celebration failed to last four full quarters in Week 11.

Quarterback Trust Meter for All 32 NFL Teams Entering the Home Stretch | Bleacher Report

New York Giants — J.J. McCarthy: 4/10. McCarthy has, at the very least, managed the offense effectively and reliably while making considerable progress in a new setting. Still, the 23-year-old’s numbers aren’t pretty. The sample size remains small for a guy who was a complete bust in Minnesota. 

Fumble-prone Giants star strikes defiant tone: ‘I’ll be here for a long time’ | NJ.com

Skattebo pushed back on the notion that he needs to put on a show Sunday with Taylor on the opposite sideline. “I wouldn’t put it like that, because he’s on a 3-7 team and I’m on a 6-3 team,” he said. “So it’s a little different, the way they’re doing things over there and the way we’re doing things over here. I’ve got to play my game. I’m not really looking to impress anybody else on the other side.”

Skattebo said he told Harbaugh this on Wednesday: “God is going to put it in our hands at some point, and this run game is going to explode. It just takes time, and it’s going to find its way.”

J.J. McCarthy on Cam Skattebo

Are the Giants frauds? Man vs. machine NFL power rankings, Week 12 | The Athletic

Oh, what to make of the New York Giants. The machines aren’t sure. I’ll be honest, I was a little surprised not to see the Giants make a bigger jump up the rankings this week — they were No. 22 last week — after they took down the machine’s fifth-ranked team, the Jacksonville Jaguars. It seems like the machines remain wary of their offense, as the Giants produced a paltry 30 percent success rate through the air and a 32 percent success rate on the ground. And while the defense played great — outside linebacker Abdul Carter was living in the Jaguars’ backfield — you have to wonder where the Giants would be ranked if the controversial no-touchdown call for Parker Washington went the other way.

item.title: 5 takeaways from the Steelers’ 27-5 win over the Denver Broncos
item.description: Takeaways, overreactions and analysis from the Steelers’ Week 12 win.
item.content:encoded:
After enduring one of the most bizarre weeks in recent NFL memory, the Steelers looked like a team that had successfully shut out the outside noise in a 27-5 win over the Denver Broncos on Black Friday.

As always, there are plenty of takeaways to be had:

1. We still have a lot to learn about the Mason Rudolph offense

Mason Rudolph delivered on Black Friday. There’s no other way to put it. Despite being thrown into the starting lineup last minute, and against one of the NFL’s better defenses, too, he hit all the hallmarks of a strong performance from a backup quarterback: some big plays, limited turnovers and sacks, and most importantly, a win.

Rudolph finished the Broncos game 9/15 for 142 yards, one touchdown, and no interceptions. He was sacked once, for a loss of 12 yards, early, but for the rest of the game stood remarkably strong in the pocket, especially when compared to his predecessor Aaron Rodgers.

Frankly, I’m not sure if Rudolph’s fourth-quarter bomb to Roman Wilson is a throw that Rodgers would’ve even attempted last week.

Still, Rudolph’s 15 passing attempts stand out like a sore thumb, especially considering that Rodgers had 73 attempts in Pittsburgh’s prior two games. Were the Steelers more run-heavy without Rodgers? From the team’s first drive alone (two passes; six runs), it’s pretty clear. But it’s also worth noting that the Steelers weren’t put in many passing situations in this game. Up 14-0 in the first quarter and 24-5 at the half in poor conditions, there was never much of a reason to air things out.

However, the Steelers’ running game wasn’t exactly great, either. Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle combined for 117 yards but a pedestrian 3.8 per carry, boosted by a 27-yard scamper by Dowdle but also brought down by a safety on a negative play and a fumble. Pittsburgh has sorely missed Mason McCormick at left guard, and Brock Hoffman has had some rough reps as of late after providing the offense with a shot of adrenaline earlier in the season.

All of that — including D.K. Metcalf finally winning a contested go ball for a score in his “random outcome generator” season — has made the Steelers’ post-Rodgers offense difficult to analyze after just one game.

Honestly, it wasn’t a great performance for the Steelers’ offense, with 14 of the team’s total 24 points coming from the defense. Pittsburgh was held to just three points in the second half.

But at the same time, Denver has a good defense. The Steelers, for much of the game, were focused on controlling the ball as much as scoring. And we can’t forget that this is a team that lost its starting quarterback — and likely a good portion of its gameplan — on Tuesday night.

At the very least, Friday’s game was another chapter in what’s turning into a memorable career for Rudolph in Pittsburgh. Ideally, it marks the start of the Steelers starting to field a more up-to-date offense without Rodgers’ many personalized preferences. But one game — especially one under such strange circumstances — is not enough to draw any meaningful conclusions.

2. Nick Herbig looks like a $100 million pass rusher

The Steelers signed Nick Herbig to a four-year, $100 million contract this summer. Then, the team decided to play him by far the least of their top three outside linebackers, and with around a quarter of his snaps coming from an alignment other than the edge.

The results haven’t reflected Herbig’s sizable new contract, with him managing just three sacks through his first nine games played of the season. He’s definitely shared some of that blame in the lack of production, but the larger problem has been Pittsburgh just not being able to maximize all three of its highly-paid rushers.

But with Alex Highsmith out against Denver, Herbig got his first shot as one of the team’s primary outside linebackers this season. He responded with a sack (and you can certainly argue that he contributed to the uncredited “team sack” where Broncos quarterback Bo Nix simply dropped the ball under pressure). He added a tackle for loss and five total tackles, flying around the field and repeatedly pressuring Nix.

The credited sack, which came against a very good tackle in Garrett Bolles, pushed the Broncos out of field goal range in the second quarter. Herbig’s tackle for loss stuffed a run on third and short. And his unreal speed for his position was a major contributor in Pittsburgh’s front repeatedly shutting down the Denver screen game on Friday.

It was just one big game. (Herbig dominated against the Buccaneers earlier this year, to be fair). But on Friday, Herbig looked well worth the Steelers’ future-facing investment in him. He was dominant versus the Broncos.

3. The Steelers defense (with some help from Bo Nix) won the game

Herbig was the biggest standout, but it was a team effort from the Steelers defense, which scored two touchdowns — that alone was enough to outscore Denver’s five points — and pitched a second-half shutout to earn a much-needed win.

Pittsburgh defensive coordinator Patrick Graham had a fantastic gameplan against Denver, forcing Nix into mistakes with heavy pressure and lots of disguising. Plus, every player on defense was prepared for the Broncos’ screen game.

Despite logging just two sacks, Pittsburgh generated a lot of pressure, and its front held a Denver run game that saw a lot of success last week to just 2.8 yards per carry. As expected, the Steelers’ athletic inside linebacker room of Patrick Queen and Payton Wilson excelled against the Broncos’ attempts to spread the defense out horizontally, but the duo also showed up coming downhill against the run and as blitzers. Both linebackers have played closer to their ceilings this year under Graham, contributing in a big way to the defense’s overall jump from 2025 to 2026.

And in the secondary, Jamel Dean, Daylen Everette and Jalen Ramsey combined for six passes defensed, nine tackles and two interceptions (Everette should’ve just batted his down on a fourth and forever, but it’s hard to ever be mad about a turnover). Denver might not have the most intimidating wide receiver room in the NFL, but it’s still a solid group and the Steelers had their tightest coverage game of the season so far.

Still, much like with the Steelers’ offense, it’s hard to know how much Pittsburgh’s defense can build on from this game. Why? Because Bo Nix put together one of the worst performances I’ve seen from a professional quarterback in a while. Both defensive touchdowns were laughably rough plays: the aforementioned dropped fumble, and then a pick six that Ramsey acknowledged was probably the easiest interception of his career.

Beyond those two plays, Nix passed for just 169 yards on 44 attempts, struggling to push the ball downfield, having accuracy issues and looking flustered by pressure. Pittsburgh dominated this one, but we’ve seen plenty of defensive struggles in recent weeks. It was a great day, but it’s rare to be gifted that many splash plays.

4. The Steelers get a big culture win

And now for the story everyone was thinking about on Friday: The big, ugly Aaron Rodgers-Mike McCarthy breakup that captivated the NFL world and left the Steelers looking like a dumpster fire ahead of a matchup with one of the AFC’s top-seeded teams.

While I’ve watched enough football to know that the “interim head coach effect” could definitely be in play against the Broncos — when a team with its back against the wall suddenly outperforms expectations — all signs pointed to this being a win for Denver against a disjointed Pittsburgh team, especially considering the Steelers’ recent two-game losing streak.

Instead, the Steelers won. In blowout fashion.

The game is already being painted as the Steelers rallying around McCarthy after a rough week, and seeing how some of Pittsburgh’s assistant coaches were reacting after the win, I wouldn’t say that’s entirely inaccurate. But even if we can all agree that Rodgers’ angry exit from Pittsburgh tarnishes his own legacy far worse than anyone else’s, the accusations against McCarthy still paint a worrying picture for the state of the 2026 Steelers. I don’t think we’ll get to the bottom of this story immediately.

A throughline of the Steelers’ postgame media appearances was that it was actually the roster’s veteran leaders, largely those on defense, who rallied the team amid a dramatic leadup to the Broncos game. That doesn’t dismiss McCarthy’s efforts, but it does point to who the most influential names on the team really are. But with McCarthy being in his first year on the team, I don’t think it’s a massive surprise or worry, either.

You’ll often see the Steelers’ group of past-their-prime greats on defense brought up when the team looks slow or unprepared in a game — usually a negative context. Against Denver, it was an undeniable positive: a group with the experience and stability to win against a playoff-caliber team despite unprecedented levels of distraction.

More than that, there seemed to be some real drive and fire to represent Pittsburgh and the Steelers after a demoralizing week for the franchise. There’s still a laundry list of long-term questions to figure out, but this win was a remarkable one for the team culture.

5. Odds and ends

  • This is the first Steeler game in some time — maybe since the beginning of the Duck Hodges era? — where it felt like watching a team with nothing to lose.
  • Al Michaels reading a rebuttal text from Aaron Rodgers live on-air was unexpected. This saga might get weirder, and while it’s darkly funny, it is sad to see one of the game’s all-time great quarterbacks go out like this.
  • Another bombshell from the Amazon broadcast: Mason Rudolph is considering a future run for senator? What a Steelers quarterback room.
  • Roman Wilson, with one catch for 37 yards on Friday, seems to be good for one long completion a game. For an up-and-down Steelers’ passing game, that’s better than nothing.
  • Germie Bernard might’ve gotten chased down a little too easily on his 58-yard catch and run, but it was still a great play by the rookie to show off some savvy against zone and his run after catch ability.
  • I’m curious if Michael Pittman Jr. will return to a bigger role in the offense in a game where Pittsburgh passes a bit more. He had just one catch for seven yards on Friday. Pat Freiermuth also only recorded one catch, while Darnell Washington was left completely off the stat sheet. But again, Rudolph only attempted 15 passes.
  • Rico Dowdle’s no-nonsense, downhill style is a great complement to Jaylen Warren, especially when the Steelers run game isn’t opening many holes.
  • Daylen Everette has been getting more slot snaps recently.
  • Safeties Robert Spears-Jennings and Jaquan Brisker are at their best coming downhill, and as a result looked great against a Broncos offense that doesn’t push the ball deep much.
  • This game was a great example for why you can never be too sure with NFL predictions. Any given… Friday, I guess?

The Steelers will get a chance to prove that the sudden resurgence against the Broncos wasn’t a fluke with another nationally-televised home game on Dec. 6’s Sunday Night Football against the Texans.

What are your takeaways from Steelers vs. Broncos? Agree/disagree with the ones above? Join the Behind the Steel Curtain community and let us know in the comments!

Kyle Shanahan, Mac Jones share final updates ahead of 49ers-Seahawks
“You just went through the first three plays in the Week Five game against Seattle. How long do you think you could name the plays in that game? Could you go up to play 15? Could you do the whole game?

Me saying right hash 47 and then him reading a play gains us about a second and a half.”

Rams poach tight end from 49ers’ practice squad

item.title: John Lynch reveals how he balances 49ers' season with draft, free agency prep
item.description: John Lynch already is looking ahead to the 2027 NFL season, balancing free agency and draft prep, while the 49ers' current season still is underway.
item.content:encoded:
John Lynch reveals how he balances 49ers' season with draft, free agency prep originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

    John Lynch already is working on next year’s roster while the 49ers currently chase Super Bowl LXI.

    The San Francisco general manager, who agreed to a multi-year contract extension just days ago, explained to NBC Sports Bay Area’s Matt Maiocco on “49ers Game Plan” how he handles both. His answer starts with how he plans his week.

    “I think your schedule has to reflect your priorities, and so I’m very intentional about my schedule,” Lynch said. “Still being around our team, getting my time with Kyle [Shannahan], going to our team meetings, going to practice.”

    Lynch and owner Jed York reportedly reached the extension on the sideline before Sunday night’s win over the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City. Lynch’s previous contract was set to expire after this season. He and coach Kyle Shanahan have led the 49ers together since 2017, and they have a 91-68 regular season record and two Super Bowl appearances.

    The in-season work, Lynch said, includes a weekly routine with his top personnel executives. Vice president of player personnel Tariq Ahmad scouts on the road each week, then returns for a day of film with Lynch and assistant general manager RJ Gillen, and Josh Williams, the director of scouting and football operations.

    “Tariq Ahmad is out on the road every week, but comes in on Tuesday, and we watch college film all day,” Lynch said. “And I do that with RJ Gillen and Josh Williams.”

    The pro personnel department is also looking ahead, he said, even though the coaches are not.

    “So just today, you know, still the pro department, who’s out there, who might be a free agent, we’re already turning to that for next year,” Lynch said. “Coaches aren’t, but we are, and that’s part of our job.”

    Lynch said he splits the work into manageable pieces, so there is no scramble when the offseason arrives.

    “You just divide it up and take it in small chunks. Sometimes you take it in large chunks, such that when you get there, it’s not like you’re cramming for the test,” Lynch said. “It’s an ongoing process, and it’s why you surround yourself with great people that kind of do the leg work.”

    Lynch added he also enjoys it.

    “It’s really fun. It’s fun seeing the next generation of guys,” Lynch said. “I think it’s important to say, ‘OK, here’s what’s here in college, here’s what’s here in free agency,’ and then you start to put together the whole equation and formula.”

    That approach has helped build a 9-1 team that leads the NFC. Wide receiver Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel arrived this offseason, and the 49ers added Keenan Allen by trade on Nov. 10.

    For Lynch, doing both jobs at once is the job, and the 49ers are 9-1 this season with the 2027 NFL season already underway for the general manager.
